# Backend implementation contract (M3)

> Test policy, 2026-10-22: per-test instruction limits, grants and reference CPU
> requirements were removed (#740). Each test or corpus case now has a
> 120-second wall-clock hang guard. Older counts and budget references below
> describe historical evidence, not a current gate or an outstanding grant.
> Performance remains the job of `test-perf` and `bench`.


**Status:** normative for M3. [`fast-compiler.md`](fast-compiler.md) Â§9 says *why* the backend is
shaped this way and Â§2 what it must measure; [`boundary.md`](boundary.md) says how emitted code
meets JavaScript; [`research/12-js-output-and-chunking.md`](research/12-js-output-and-chunking.md)
is the evidence for every size claim below. This document says what the code looks like.

M3 ends when `beni build` produces JavaScript that runs and the emitted output is measurably close
to what a dedicated minifier would produce. The third condition this line used to carry â a direct
call share high enough to justify keeping currying â is discharged rather than met: Â§9.3 dropped
currying on 2026-09-14, so the share is 100% by construction (Â§6).

## 1. Scope and order

The order is not negotiable and one rule sets it: **nothing is optimised before it can be run.**
`boundary.md` Â§8 puts the Node platform before the optimiser for this reason â the test suite's
second boundary is compiling a program, running it under Node and asserting what it printed, and a
backend that cannot be executed is a backend whose bugs survive a green suite.

- **M3a â emit and run.** *Shipped.* `JsIr`, the printer, codegen for the pure subset, core's
  foreign JavaScript for what that subset uses, a minimal Node platform, and the harness boundary
  that runs emitted code. *Acceptance: a beni program computes something and prints the right
  answer* â `tests/corpus/run/` is 26 programs that do, executed under Node. All 65 of core's
  foreign values are implemented, not only the ones the subset reaches. `?` was the one construct
  of Â§4's table M3a did not compile, and it said so with a diagnostic rather than emitting
  something wrong.
- **M3b â the whole language.** Tail-call loops, decision trees, interpolation, `?`, tuples, record
  update, `Int32`, everything remaining. *Acceptance: the corpus compiles and runs.* **Four of the
  seven were stale when the list was written** and one is not a backend item at all: interpolation,
  tuples and record update worked in M3a (`plans/m3b-audit.md` measured every row of Â§4 against the
  code), and tail-call loops (Â§8), decision trees (Â§7) and `?` (Â§4) have landed since. **`Int32` landed on 2026-09-19 and the list is spent.** It was a *language* gap
  and never a codegen one â no type, no `core` module, no paragraph in `language.md` â and what
  built it is `core/Int32.beni` with its sibling, `language.md` Â§2.5 and Appendix A, and
  `checker.md` Appendix B's signature list. The emitter needed **no change at all**: an `Int32` is
  a number, its operations are ordinary `foreign` calls, and `==`/`<` on one resolve through the
  module rule to the module's own `pub eq`/`pub compare` like any other type's.
- **M3c â the optimiser.** Reachability elimination, reachability-driven inlining, local
  dead-binding elimination, renaming, field ambiguation, compact printing. *Acceptance: Â§9's size
  and throughput numbers, and Â§9's size and throughput numbers alone; the direct-call share that used to decide Â§9.3 is
  discharged, not measured (Â§6).* **Reachability elimination is built first and is not optional**:
  static dispatch derives eagerly, so an empty program ships 3 159 bytes of `eq`/`compare` that
  nothing calls, and `fast-compiler.md` Â§13 moved this pass from an optimisation to a prerequisite
  on that evidence. Its own acceptance is separate and exact: the floor's `derived_bytes` is **0**
  for a program that compares nothing (Â§9).

  **M3c ships in two slices, and the first one is what `--release` means.** The first is Â§9 items
  **1, 2, 3 and 5** â local dead-binding elimination, short names, compact printing and variable
  joining â together with the flag itself; it is one pass over `JsIr`, one name table and one
  printer boolean, and it stands alone because none of the four needs anything the backend does not
  already have. The second is item **4**, type-directed field ambiguation, which needs an artifact
  Â§3 says the backend does not receive, plus anything chunk-facing (Â§10). Sliced that way because
  the first is worth a measured **31% of `bench/corpus`'s compressed bytes** and the second is
  worth report 12's 4% (Â§9), and because a `--release` that is refused is worse than a `--release`
  that is not yet perfect. The one entry in this bullet's own list that is in neither slice is
  **"reachability-driven inlining"**, which was never a Â§9 item and has no measurement behind it;
  what Â§9 now specifies under item 1 is single-use inlining of the temporaries Â§4, Â§7 and Â§8
  generate, which is a different and measured thing.
- **M3d â chunking and `lazy`.** The keyword, entry-set colouring, the merge pass, cross-chunk
  bindings. *Acceptance: a two-route program splits and both routes run.*

  **The two halves have a dependency between them and it is not small.** Â§10 specifies the chunker;
  the keyword is PENDING an owner decision, because a deferred load is asynchronous, the language is
  synchronous, and `fast-compiler.md` Â§9.5's type rewrite names a `Task` that
  `transparent-effects-proposal.md` removes. [`plans/m3d-plan.md`](../../plans/m3d-plan.md) Â§2 is the
  argument, Â§6 the decisions â including what "route" means on a platform whose only entry point is
  `main`, and whether the chunker ships against multiple entry points before `lazy` exists.

`boundary.md`'s B1 and B2 fold into M3a; B3 through B5 follow M3d.

## 2. CLI surface

```
beni build [options] <entry>...      compile to JavaScript
```

| Flag | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--platform=<name>` | which platform package supplies `main`'s type and the runtime | required |
| `--release` | dead bindings out, short names, compact printing, joined `const`s (Â§9); **refuses a build that reaches `Debug`**; later chunks (Â§10), integer tags, maps off | off |
| `--library` | no `main` is required and no entry file is written; every name the root package's modules export is a reachability root (Â§9) | off |
| `--out=<dir>` | output directory | `out/` |
| `--source-maps` | a `.mjs.map` beside every emitted module (Â§11.1), or beside every file a release build lowers from beni (Â§11.2); a map embeds the beni source text (`sourcesContent`); `--no-source-maps` writes none | on in dev; off with `--release`, which writes maps only when the flag is given |

*Amended 2026-10-01: development source maps are built (Â§11.1).* A development build writes a map
beside every module by default; `--source-maps` states that default and `--no-source-maps` turns
it off (both together exit 2). The refusal described next survives for `--release` only:
`--release --source-maps` exits 2 with `beni: --source-maps is not implemented for --release yet; a
release build writes no .map file`, by the same argument, and `--release` alone writes no map. The
two paragraphs below are kept as the record of why.

*Amended 2026-10-15: release maps are built (Â§11.2).* `--release --source-maps` is no longer
refused: it writes a map for each file that the release build lowers from beni. `--release` alone
still writes no map, and `--release --no-source-maps` states that default. The refusal and its two
paragraphs below are history now.

**`--source-maps` is refused, not ignored.** It is not implemented â the encoder is M5 (Â§11) â and a
flag that is accepted while doing nothing makes a user believe they asked for something: a silent,
successful `--source-maps` build sends them looking for a `.map` that was never written, exactly as a
silent `--release` build would have shipped development output. It exits `2` with `frontend.md` Â§1's
one-line usage message naming the milestone. The defaults in the table above are what M5 will do;
until then the only way to build is without that flag. `--release` was refused on the same argument
and no longer is, because the optimiser's first slice implements it.

**`--release` stopped being refused with the optimiser's first slice, and `--source-maps` did not.** The
refusal was one branch (`src/Cli.zig:362-364`); it went, the `release: bool` already parsed at
`:338-341` reaches `Emit.Options`, and the usage line at `:46` states what the flag does rather than
what it does not. Nothing else about the command changed: `--release` takes no value, composes with
`--library` and `--out` and `--jobs` exactly as `--library` does, and **implies nothing** â in
particular it does not switch elimination on, because elimination is always on (Â§9), and it does not
switch source maps off, because there are none to switch. `--source-maps` keeps its own refusal at
`:369-371` and keeps it in a `--release` build too, so the pair `--release --source-maps` exits 2 on
the source-map line. The one thing it changes beyond Â§9's four passes: the entry file's two-line
header comment goes, which is 135 bytes of the floor's 2 009. `dump --stage=â¦` is untouched for the same reason Â§9 gives: every stage is
before the backend.

**`--release` does refuse one thing, and it is not a flag: a build that reaches `Debug`** (the
owner's decision, 2026-09-19; the rule and the reasons are Â§9's *The release optimiser*, under *`Debug`
is refused, not pinned*). It exits `1` with `debug_in_release`, writes nothing to `--out`, and names
the use sites. That is Elm's rule for `--optimize`, and it is what lets this section's "a release
build behaves exactly as the development build does" stand with no exception. It is a refusal of a
PROGRAM and not of a flag, so unlike `--source-maps` it is a diagnostic on stderr and exit `1`
rather than a usage line and exit `2`.

**There is a third hidden flag, `--allow-debug`** (`src/Cli.zig`, alongside `--roundtrip-interfaces`
and `--iface-hash`), absent from the table above and from `beni help` for their reason: it is
diagnostic surface, not product surface. It turns that refusal off and changes nothing else â not
one emitted byte, in either mode. It exists because `Debug.log` is the corpus's only instrument for
observing evaluation order and the `--release` second pass over `run/` is what proved the wide
inliner unsafe (Â§9 item 1); a refusal with no way past it would silently stop 24 of the 121 fixtures
from being built in release at all. `tests/corpus/build/bad-release/` is the kind that does NOT pass
it. **Development output does not move by one byte** â every `emit/` golden, every
`run/` `.expected` and every `bench/size.mjs` figure in this document is a dev-build figure and stays
one â which is what makes "a golden moved" a finding rather than a blessing for the whole slice.

**`--library` is not in that company**: it lands with Â§9 and does something the day it lands. It
turns off exactly two things â the REQUIREMENT for a `main` (`missing_main` does not fire, a second
`main` is not a `duplicate_main`, and a `main` that is there is not checked against the platform's
`Program`)
and the entry file â and turns on one, the root rule. A `main` that happens to exist is still
exported and still a root, because Â§5's export list has the entry declaration in it and Â§9 roots a
library at its export list; Â§9's "Roots" says why at length. It is not a second output mode; a
library build emits the same `.mjs` per module as any other.

Development output is **one ESM file per source module**, mirroring the source tree, with readable
names â but not with everything the source declared. Release output is **reachability chunks**. Both
read one declaration graph (Â§9.1 of the design doc) and **both eliminate against it**: a dev build
and a release build ship the same set of declarations and differ in how those are named, laid out
and grouped into files. Nothing is built twice. Â§5.3 of `boundary.md` makes a build a pair of entry
point and platform, so a project with a client and a server runs `build` twice.
*Amended 2026-09-30:* until Â§10's chunks exist, a release APPLICATION is one file, the entry file,
holding every module, sibling and runtime of the program in one module scope (Â§9, *One scope-hoisted
file under `--release`*); a release `--library` build keeps one `.mjs` per module.

**Elimination is not behind a flag**, and Â§9 gives the reason: eager derivation makes it the
difference between an empty program shipping 70 kB and shipping 2 kB, and a development build that
ships fifty times what it needs is not a development build anyone would run. What `--library`
changes is the root SET and never whether the pass runs.

A successful build prints **nothing, on either stream**. `frontend.md` Â§1 gives stdout to the product
and stderr to diagnostics and nothing else; a build's product is the files it wrote, so there is no
stream left for a summary line, and `check` already sets the precedent. How much was written is a
`--self-profile` counter (`emitted_files`, `emitted_bytes`), which is also where the incrementality
tests read "this edit rewrote one file".

File extension is `.mjs`, so nothing depends on a `package.json` the user owns. **That applies to
every file a build writes, the hand-written ones included** â the first backend shipped copying core's siblings
and the platform's runtime out as `.js`, and Node then reparsed each one and warned
`MODULE_TYPELESS_PACKAGE_JSON` on every start, whose own suggested remedy is adding `"type":
"module"` to a `package.json`. That is the dependency this rule exists to avoid, arriving through
the back door. (*Amended 2026-09-28:* the rule is about files that are LOADED; the one
file a build writes that is not a module, `_manifest.txt` â *The output directory holds what the
last build wrote* below â is not `.mjs` and is never imported. *Amended 2026-10-01:* nor is a
development build's `<module>.mjs.map` (Â§11.1), which a debugger reads and nothing imports.) A copied file cannot simply keep its stem, because `out/_core/List.mjs` is already the
generated module, so it takes **`.foreign.mjs`**: it says which half of the module it is, and it
cannot collide â a generated file is named for its module, every segment of a module name is an
upper identifier, so no generated file has two dots in its base name. The `.js` names in `core/` and
`platforms/` on disk are unchanged; `language.md` Â§5.4 fixes the sibling's NAME and not its
extension, and only the copy is executed.

The rename has one consequence the backend refuses rather than gets wrong: **a sibling may not import
another FILE.** `import { cons } from "./List.js"` is written against a name the copy no longer has,
and rewriting the specifier is not done. A bare specifier â `node:process`, a package â survives the
copy untouched and is what `boundary.md` Â§4's third check is really about, so nothing that check
blesses is lost today except sharing a helper file between two siblings. The `not_implemented` this
raises **points at the specifier itself, inside the `.js`**, by `boundary.md` Â§4's *a diagnostic
points at the file whose text is wrong*; it used to land on the first `foreign` declaration of the
module beside it, which is a line nobody would think to look at.

**No `package.json` is written into the output, and that is deliberate.** `.mjs` already makes every
file an ES module whatever any `package.json` says, so one would add nothing â and it would put back
exactly the file the extension was chosen to avoid, inside a directory the user chose (`--out` may
well point at something they own). A build writes only files it named itself.

### The output directory holds what the last build wrote, and nothing it wrote before

*Added 2026-09-28.* Until then a build only ever ADDED to `--out`: build a
`Main` importing `Half` and `Dict`, then a `Main` using neither into the same directory, and
`out/Half.mjs`, `out/_core/Dict.mjs` and their siblings survived beside a program that never
wrote them â stale modules a reader of `out/`, a bundler globbing it, or a deploy copying it
all take for part of the program.

**The rule: after a successful build, the files of `--out` that beni wrote are exactly the files
a build of the same program into an empty directory writes.** A file an earlier build wrote and
this one does not is removed, and so is a directory the removal leaves empty. Nothing else in
`--out` is touched: `--out` may well be a directory the user owns (the `package.json` paragraph
above), and a file beni did not write is never beni's to delete.

**What beni wrote is recorded, not inferred.** Every successful build writes a manifest,
`_manifest.txt`, at the root of `--out` â a reserved name by rule 1 below, and one no platform
`"entry"` can take because an entry name ends in `.mjs`. Its first line is `beni-manifest 1`;
each further line is one file the build wrote, as `<hash> <path>`: the path relative to `--out`
with `/` separators, in write order, and the hash the 64-bit Wyhash of the bytes written, as 16
lower-case hex digits. The manifest itself is not listed and is not counted in `emitted_files`.
A stale file is removed only when **all** of these hold, and is left alone otherwise, silently:

1. the previous manifest lists it, and this build does not write it;
2. its path is relative, `/`-separated, and has no empty, `.` or `..` segment â a manifest is a
   file in a directory anyone can edit, and a line that could name something outside `--out` is
   not acted on;
3. its bytes still hash to what the manifest recorded. A file the user has since edited is
   theirs now, and survives;
4. *(added 2026-09-28)* it is not **the same file** as one this build
   writes. `Ab.mjs` from the last build and `AB.mjs` from this one are one file on APFS and NTFS:
   comparing paths byte for byte read the file just written there, found the old hash whenever
   the bytes agreed (two `--release` modules of identical content do), and deleted it. So a stale
   path equal to a written one under ASCII case folding â the folding rule 2 of the next
   subsection uses â is removed only when the file system reports the two names as two files
   (different inode numbers); if either cannot be stat'd, it stays. On a case-sensitive file
   system they are two, the older one goes, and `--out` still matches a fresh build.

*Amended 2026-09-28.* A manifest must be beni's to be acted on OR
overwritten. `_manifest.txt` is beni's when its first line is `beni-manifest 1` and every
further line is `<16 hex digits> <path>`, the file ending in a newline. A file of that name in
any other shape â the user's own notes, a future version's format, one that cannot be read â is
somebody else's: the build is **refused** with `unknown_output_record`, naming the file, before
the first byte is written, and `--out` is left as it was. (Until the amendment such a file read
as an empty manifest and was silently overwritten.) A well-formed line whose path fails rule 2
is still only skipped, never refused: the manifest is beni's, edited, and the one thing ruled
out is acting on that line. With no manifest at all â the first build into a directory, or a
directory from before this rule â nothing is removed.

*Amended 2026-09-29.* A `_manifest.txt` that exists and **cannot be read** is no longer called
somebody else's: whose it is cannot be told, and `unknown_output_record`'s "does not begin with
`beni-manifest 1`" was a claim nobody could check. The build fails as it does for any file it
cannot read â `beni: cannot read 'out/_manifest.txt': AccessDenied`, exit 2 â still before the
first byte is written, and `--out` is left as it was.

*Amended 2026-09-29: beni writes through no symbolic link.* beni makes no link in `--out`, so one
there is somebody else's, and writing its path writes wherever it points â outside `--out`,
possibly. A dangling `_manifest.txt` link read as no manifest, and the build wrote the manifest
through it; a `_main.mjs` link had the entry file written over its target. Before the first byte
is written, every path the build would write â the manifest and each output â is examined under
`--out` component by component without following links, and the first link on each is refused
with `unknown_output_record`, naming the link (and, for a directory, the file the build would
write inside it). Nothing is written. `--out` itself may be a link: the user named it. A write
that fails names the file that failed: the manifest's is `out/_manifest.txt`, not `out`.

**Deploying `--out`.** `_manifest.txt` is served next to the modules unless the deploy excludes
it; it lists the path and a content hash of every file the build wrote (modules, copied
siblings, the runtime and the entry file), and nothing else. *(Added 2026-09-28.)*

**The order makes an interrupted build safe.** Before the first output byte, the manifest is
rewritten as the old entries followed by the new ones (the union, so a build killed halfway still
lists every file either build may have written). Then the outputs are written, then the stale
files removed, then the manifest rewritten with this build's entries alone.

**A refused build changes nothing** â no output, no removal, no manifest â for the reason the
checks of *The output tree does not depend on the file system's case sensitivity* run before the
first byte: a build that says it failed leaves `--out` exactly as the last successful build left
it.

### The output tree does not depend on the file system's case sensitivity

**A build's output is the same set of files on every file system.** That is the guarantee, and it
is worth stating because it was not true. macOS (APFS) and Windows (NTFS) fold case by default, so
two output paths that differ only by case are ONE file there: whichever is written second wins, and
the build exits `0` having shipped something that throws at load. Until 2026-09-21 the entry file
was `main.mjs` and the conventional entry module `Main.beni` emitted `Main.mjs` beside it â the same
file on a case-insensitive system, the shim written second, so `out/Main.mjs` imported itself and
every program built on a Mac died with `SyntaxError: does not provide an export named 'Main$main'`.
31 of 277 `test-blackbox` cases failed there, all of them that.

Two rules make it unreachable, and both are checks rather than conventions.

**Rule 1 â a reserved output name begins with `_`, which no module path can.** A module is named by
its path with `/` for `.` (`language.md` Â§5), and every segment must be an upper identifier, which
begins with an ASCII capital letter (`SourceStore.isUpperIdent`). A leading `_` is therefore a
region of the name space no module can reach, under case folding or otherwise â unlike a suffix or
a subdirectory, which only moves the collision. The reserved names are:

| Reserved | What it is | Was |
|---|---|---|
| `_main.mjs` | the entry file (Â§5, `boundary.md` Â§5.2), unless the platform declares another name | `main.mjs` |
| `_core/` | the `core` package's directory | `core/` |
| `_platform/` | the platform package's directory, holding its modules, their siblings and its runtime | `platform/` |
| `_manifest.txt` | the list of files the last build wrote (*The output directory holds what the last build wrote*) | â |

All three were reachable before: `Main.beni` lands on `Main.mjs`, a user module `Core.List` on
`Core/List.mjs`, `Platform.Node` on `Platform/Node.mjs`. Only the first had been hit.

Inside `_core/`, a `_` name is the emitter's own for the same reason: `_core/_derived.mjs` is the
derived-comparison runtime (Â§4, *Derived comparisons do not grow the native stack*), which no core
module file (an upper name) can take.

**A platform MAY declare the entry file's name**, which is `boundary.md` Â§5.2's *"a platform
declares its output shape â¦ rather than hardcoding one"* finished for the one part of the shape that
was still hardcoded: the manifest's `"entry"` key. A declared name is subject to rule 1 and is
checked when the platform is loaded â one path segment, beginning with `_`, ending in `.mjs`, with
ASCII letters, digits, `_` or `-` between. Anything else is `invalid_entry_file`, reported against
the manifest at `1:1` with no excerpt, the shape `foreign_sibling_missing` uses for a fault that is
about a file rather than a place inside one. **Declaring the name is not on its own the fix**: a
platform that declared `main.mjs` would put the defect straight back, which is why the rule is
enforced and not documented.

**A platform MAY declare that the entry file exports what `run` returns** (*added 2026-10-21*;
`boundary.md` Â§5.2's `"exports"` key, Â§9.12 (c)). With `"exports": "program"` in the chain, the entry
file binds `run(main)`'s result as `$beniProgram`, writes its `default` as the default export, and
writes one named export per name the app's `beni.json` lists under `"exports"`, each the answer of
the result's `exports(name)`, as `const $beniExport<N> = â¦; export { $beniExport<N> as Name };` in
the list's order; the hoisted `--release` file does the same at its end. The entry's own bindings
are longer than any short name `Rename` spells (eight characters), so no hoisted declaration can
collide with them; a listed name is written only as an export name, a namespace of its own that no
binding meets, so a listed `$beniProgram` is legal and loads. A name that is not an ASCII
identifier name, is `default`, is `flush` or is listed twice is `invalid_entry_export`, against
the app's manifest at `1:1`; any other mode is `unknown_exports_mode`, against the platform's; a
list on a chain that declares no mode is the warning `exports_ignored`. `flush` is refused because
the hoisted release file re-exports the runtime's `flush` when the build keeps it (Â§15.11), and a
module that exports one name twice does not load (`SyntaxError: Duplicate export`); the refusal is
static, the same in both builds, where a test of the runtime's exports would follow reachability
and differ between them. `stop` is not refused: only a runtime module supplies it, and the exports
mode refuses a runtime module. A chain whose runtime is a module (`boundary.md` Â§9.2) may not
declare the key yet: the same `unknown_exports_mode`, found from the chain alone, so `check`, a
development build and a release build refuse it alike. A listed name is ASCII only â letters,
digits, `_` and `$` â although an export name may be any identifier name, a reserved word
included: the name is printed into the entry file without escaping, as the entry file's name is,
and the ASCII rule is what makes the print safe.
**The runtime's `exports(name)` must throw for a name the program does not define**, with a
message that names it, never return `undefined`: the entry file calls it unguarded, once at load
(rule 9), so a silent `undefined` would ship as `export { undefined as Name }`, and no check of
the compiler's sees it. `run/EntryExports` pins the shape and the order,
`build/bad/UnknownExportsMode`, `build/bad/ExportsListOnPlatform`, `build/bad/ExportsWithRuntimeModule`,
`build/bad/InvalidEntryExport` and `build/bad/FlushEntryExport` the refusals, `run/ExportsIgnored` the
warning; `tests/blackbox/build_test.zig` runs the runtime-module chain under `--release` and `check`,
which the corpus's `build/bad/` kind does not.

**Rule 2 â two output paths equal under case folding is a build error.** It is the backstop for
whatever rule 1 does not reach, and one case is not exotic at all: two modules whose paths differ
only by case â `Json.Decode` and `JSON.Decode` â are two modules on Linux and one file on macOS.
Folding is **simple ASCII lower-casing**, nothing more: every module name segment is an ASCII upper
identifier and the compiler's own reserved names are ASCII, so there is no Unicode case folding to
perform and none is performed.

The check runs over the list of files the build is about to write, **after everything is produced
and before the first byte is written**, so a refused build leaves nothing behind exactly as
`boundary.md` Â§4's checks do. The list is built in module order, which is file-index order (`fast-compiler.md` Â§10) and
never completion order (CLAUDE.md rule 5), so the pair reported is the same at every `--jobs`. The
diagnostic is `output_path_collision`; it names both output paths and the two files they came from,
because the fault is in neither one alone.

**It is a check of what is WRITTEN, not of what exists**, and that is the one place it differs from
Â§4. Â§5's *Elimination decides what is written, never what is checked* is about a contract on
privileged code, which holds whether or not anything imports it; this is a property of the output
tree, so a module the reachability walk dropped cannot collide with anything, because it is not
there. The guarantee is about the artifact, and the artifact is what survived.

**What this costs to test, and why one fixture cannot exist.** A corpus fixture for rule 2's
headline case would need `Json/Decode.beni` and `JSON/Decode.beni` checked into the repository, and
those are one file on the very systems the rule is for â the repository would not survive a
checkout on a Mac. So the collision is provoked two other ways: a platform whose runtime and whose
sibling land on the same output name (constructible everywhere, because the two SOURCE paths differ
by more than case), and a harness invariant that folds the written-file list after every build the
black-box suite makes. The second is the one that would have caught this defect on Linux, where the
file system hides it, and it costs nothing per case (Â§12).

### The page shell, `index.html`

*Added 2026-10-01* (Milestone 1's developer loop, `frontend.md` Â§10). A browser program is a module
graph, and a module graph does nothing until a page loads its entry with `<script type="module">`.
Until now the developer wrote that page by hand; **the platform now declares it**, as it declares
the entry file's name (`boundary.md` Â§5.2), because which page loads a program is part of the
artifact's shape and differs by platform â `node` has none.

- **The key.** A platform manifest's `"html"` names a template file relative to its package root;
  like every output key it is inherited field by field down the chain (`boundary.md` Â§9.1), so
  `browser` declares it and `browser-tea` gets it. The **app's** `beni.json` may name its own, relative
  to the manifest's directory (`frontend.md` Â§10.1), and then it replaces the chain's: that is how a
  project adds a stylesheet, a title or a mount element without a compiler change.
- **The placeholders.** The template is copied byte for byte except that every `{{entry}}` becomes
  the base and the entry file's name â `/_main.mjs` by default, or what the platform's `"entry"` and
  the project's `"base"` say â and every `{{base}}` the base alone. **`{{entry}}` must
  occur at least once**: a page that never loads the program is a build that succeeded and does
  nothing, the silent wrong answer this project refuses, so a template without it is
  `invalid_html_shell`, reported against the template at `1:1` with no excerpt. A template that
  cannot be read is the same code, reported against the manifest that named it. More than one
  occurrence is allowed â it is the author's page.
- **The output.** It is written as `index.html` at the root of `--out`, through `pending` like every
  other output, so rule 2's folding check, the `_manifest.txt` record and stale-file removal all
  apply to it unchanged. **`index.html` needs no `_`**: rule 1 is about names a MODULE can take, and
  every module's output ends in `.mjs`, so no module can reach a `.html` name under any folding.
- **When.** Only for a program build: a `--library` build writes no entry file, so it has nothing
  to load and writes no page. A chain and an app that name no `"html"` write none, so a `node` build's
  tree does not move by a file.
- **Development and `--release` write the same page.** The release entry is still one file with the
  same name, so the page is identical; nothing is inlined. No live-reload script is ever in it â that
  is `beni serve`'s, injected into the HTTP response and never written (`frontend.md` Â§10.4).
- **Deterministic**: the bytes are a function of the template, the entry name and the base alone.
- **Absolute, from the base** (*amended 2026-10-01, the manager's decision before merge*). The
  entry path is the project's `"build"."base"` (`frontend.md` Â§10.1) followed by the entry file's
  name, and the base defaults to `/`, so the page loads `/_main.mjs`. An absolute path is what makes
  a single-page app's nested routes work out of the box: `/todos/3`, answered with this page by
  `beni serve`'s fallback or a host's rewrite rule, still loads `/_main.mjs` â a relative
  `./_main.mjs`, the first draft, resolved to `/todos/_main.mjs` and loaded nothing. Routing is next
  on the roadmap and base `/` is the common default (Vite's). An app hosted under a sub-path says so
  once, `"base": "/app/"`; a template may also write `{{base}}` for its own links
  (`{{base}}favicon.ico`). A base must end in `/` â `/app` would make `/app_main.mjs` â and may not
  hold a quote, `<`, `>` or whitespace, which would end the attribute it is written into; anything
  else is an exit-2 line naming the value (`frontend.md` Â§10.1).

## 3. `JsIr` â the second IR

Â§9.2 settles that there are two IRs and not one: lowering the typed IR straight to a byte buffer was
measured as neutral in Elm and loses the ability to pattern-match on generated structure, which is
what the peephole and specialisation passes need.

`JsIr` is a `MultiArrayList` of fixed-size nodes with one `extra: []u32` sidecar and `enum(u32)`
indices, exactly as every other IR here (Â§5). It is JavaScript-shaped, not beni-shaped: statements
and expressions, `var`/`const` declarations, function expressions, calls, member access, object and
array literals, `switch`, labelled `while`, `return`, conditional expressions. It carries **source
positions from the start** even while maps are off (Â§9.6), because retrofitting them touches every
pass.

Names in `JsIr` are `Symbol`s, never strings, so renaming in the optimiser is a table swap rather than a
rewrite.

**The backend still sees no types, and static dispatch did not change that.** `Lower.Input` gains
one field beside `interfaces`: a **dispatch table**, one per module, flat and index-based in the
shape of `Bir.refs`, in which the checker has already written what every method call resolved to,
what evidence every declaration takes, and which functions must be derived. The lowerer reads
targets, never types. â [`static-dispatch-spike.md`](static-dispatch-spike.md) Â§7, Â§8.0.

**The elimination graph is not `JsIr`'s.** Â§9's reachability walk runs over `Bir` and the dispatch
table *before* lowering, so an unreachable declaration never becomes `JsIr` nodes at all and `JsIr`
holds only what survives. That is the opposite of Â§9 item 1, the local dead-binding pass, which is a
use-count walk over `JsIr` after lowering and removes bindings *inside* a declaration that is being
emitted. Two passes, two IRs, and neither is a fallback for the other. `Lower.Input` gains one more
field for it (Â§9).

*Amended 2026-10-20 (the owner's decision D1, issue #488; `plans/type-directed-points-to.md` Â§3):*
**the backend receives one artifact of types, and lowering does not read it.** Beside the dispatch
table, `Lower.Input` carries per module a **type-key artifact**: a key for every Bir local and for
every allocating instruction (a record literal or update, a constructor application, a tuple, a list
literal, a lambda), and the closed types the module adds to fact 3's wild set (Â§9). A key is the
canonical form of a closed type: a nominal type's `TypeId` with its arguments' keys, a record as its
fields' (symbol, key) pairs sorted by symbol, a tuple as its arity and elements' keys, a function as
its parameters' keys and its result's. An alias is the type it names, so an alias and its structure
have one key. A key is **wild** when the type holds a type variable or a row variable, a `foreign
type` (`Js.Value` and `Js.Ref` among them), or the schema `Value` (`schema.md` A.6), and anything
the compiler makes with no Bir local or instruction of its own has no key and is wild. The checker
computes the keys in `Module.check` while the module's store and `local_type` still exist, before
the store is freed (`checker-v2.md` Â§5), in every build, so that a cache entry written by a
development build serves a release one. The keys are written into the cache entry as a sixth
section, `type_keys`, holding each key as a canonical term; `entry_bytes`' format goes from 11 to 12
(`checker-v2.md` Â§14.3, `schema.md` A.6). **The artifact never decides what lowering emits**:
`Lower` maps each type key to a representation key and writes it into two columns beside the nodes,
`JsIr.name_key` and `JsIr.node_key`, and the one reader of those columns is fact 3's declared-type
filter (Â§9, *Declared-type filtering of fact 3*). A module's keys are the same whether it was
checked in this build or read from the cache, so the output never depends on a warm cache, and the
warm/cold pair that tests it is one of the slice's fixtures. Key ids are assigned at the merge in
module order from the canonical terms, never by a worker (rule 5). **In the first version every key
of a `core` module and of a platform module is wild**: the checked core shipped in the binary is
never checked again. Their interfaces still carry the one bit Â§9 asks of every module, whether a
quantifier crosses into JavaScript. This is the one place the backend sees a type; Â§9's
field-interference artifact (*Item 4 â field ambiguation, specified and then declined*) stays
declined.

*Amended 2026-10-22:* record-row field sets now also cross in this artifact
(checker-v2.md Â§36) and feed release field colouring (Â§9, *Item 4, taken up*).
They do not require closed field-value types; unknown rows are conservative.
This supersedes the withdrawal of field-interference facts above.

## 4. Codegen, construct by construct

Representation decisions are Â§9.4's and are not reopened here. What this section fixes is the
mapping.

| beni | JavaScript |
|---|---|
| top-level value | one `const` per declaration, module-qualified name in dev, short name in release |
| function of *n* parameters | one function expression of arity *n*; no arity tag (Â§6) |
| a pattern in an irrefutable position | a fresh name plus a destructuring statement, **with no test** â a parameter, a `let` pattern and a `<-` bound pattern alike. Correct by construction: `language.md` Â§7 makes all of them irrefutable, the parser refusing the shapes no type can rescue and `checker.md` Â§6.6 refusing a constructor whose type has more than one, so a pattern that could fail never reaches lowering. A single-constructor type destructures through whichever shape Â§9.4 gave it â `{$: "Tag", a, b}`, or the bare tag when its one constructor is nullary |
| saturated call at known arity | direct call `f(a, b)` (Â§6) |
| record | object literal, keys in a canonical sorted order so one hidden class per record type â the sort moves the **keys** and never an initialiser (below) |
| constructor | `{$: tag, a, b}` padded to a uniform shape per type; tag is a string in dev, an integer in release. *Amended 2026-10-01:* an integer only for a type no JavaScript sees, and never `Order` â Â§9, *Item 4, taken up* |
| record-alias constructor | the **record literal** it builds, as the record row above: `P 1 "a"` for `type alias P = { x : Int, y : String }` is `{x: 1, y: "a"}`, keys in the canonical sorted order and the arguments evaluated in written order, with no tag â the value IS a `{ x : Int, y : String }` (`language.md` Â§0, Elm's semantics; the owner's decision that a record alias constructor builds the record, `checker-v2.md` Â§21). Unapplied or partially applied it is the same wrapper any constructor gets, `(a, b) => ({x: a, y: b})`. As a **pattern** (`nameOf (P n _) = n`) it is irrefutable â one constructor â and reads argument `i` as the alias's field `i` in declaration order, `.x` then `.y`, with no test (decided 2026-09-24 under rule 7). An **imported** alias's constructor is the same record, built and read by the field names interface v3's `record_alias` constructor row carries (`checker-v2.md` Â§14.2): until 2026-09-25 it was `not_implemented`, because interface v2 had no names |
| nullary constructor | the bare tag â or, for a type that also has a constructor with fields, one module-level constant object per constructor (*A nullary constructor is one object*, below; 2026-09-29) |
| tuple | fixed-shape object per arity, no runtime tag |
| list | cons cells (`{$:1, a, b}` / the empty singleton), pending a benchmark of a vector trie. A literal of more than 32 elements is ONE array whose cells `reduceRight` builds (*Emitted JavaScript nests only as deep as the source*, below). *Amended 2026-10-01, the owner's decision (W35):* **a list is array-backed** â a plain JavaScript array, a view, or a 32-way trie with a claimable tail; *Lists are arrays*, below, is the contract, and it replaces this row when `plans/list-arrays.md`'s second slice lands. *Amended 2026-10-01 again (W35, E1tp):* the trie has a claimable **head** as well, so prepending is as cheap as appending (*The claimable head: E1tp*, below). *Amended 2026-10-11, the owner:* the head is no longer claimable and a prepend copies; the head survives only as what a prefix removal leaves of the tree's first leaf (the same subsection's amendment) |
| string | native JavaScript string; core's API exposes codepoints where the UTF-16 mismatch would show |
| `Int` | a number |
| `Int32` | **a number too** â an ordinary JavaScript number held in signed 32-bit range by every operation that produces one, with no box and no tag, so `toInt` is the identity and the whole cost of the type is the `\| 0` (ECMA-262's ToInt32) that keeps the invariant true. `mul` is `Math.imul` and `shiftRightZero` is `(x >>> n) \| 0`, because `>>>` answers unsigned. The type exists in beni and not at run time, which is what makes it free; `core/Int32.js` and this row are the contract (`fast-compiler.md` Â§3.1, `checker.md` Appendix B). *(Amended 2026-10-01: `core/Int32.beni` is, written over `Js` â `plans/core-in-beni.md` â and has no sibling.)* |
| `case` | a decision tree (Â§7) |
| `if` | conditional expression when both arms are expressions, else `if`/`else` |
| `let` | a VALUE binding is a `const` in the enclosing statement list, in written order; a binding whose right-hand side is a **function** is a `function` declaration, which JavaScript **hoists** â every one of them, not only the mutually recursive ones. The hoisting is what makes mutual recursion between `let` functions work, and `language.md` Â§7's initialisation rule is stated in terms of it: a value may not read a `const` below it, and may read a `function` anywhere |
| string interpolation | template literal. *Amended 2026-10-17:* a segment that is a call of core's `String.fromInt` is its argument, `${n}` for `${String.fromInt n}`: a template converts a number to the text `String` gives it, and an `Int` is a number (`Lower.fromIntArgument`, keyed on core's module and name). `String.fromFloat` is not: it writes a whole float with its point |
| `?` | a test and an early `return` of the failure, in statements, over the subject bound once (below) |
| `foreign` | an `import` from the sibling file, one binding per foreign value (`boundary.md` Â§4). Its **arity is its annotation's**, carried on the declaration's `params` by lowering (`frontend.md` Â§3.6): the backend reads targets and never types (Â§3), so a `foreign` in value position eta-expands over that number like any other target |
| method call, resolved to a declaration | a direct call of that declaration, receiver first: `x.m a` is `M$m(x, a)` |
| method call on a `primitive` target | the JavaScript operator the surface origin names â `===` for `==`, and the `Order` result of `compare` tested in place rather than built |
| return-type dispatch | a direct call of whatever the constrained variable resolved to, or of the evidence parameter standing in for it |
| a declaration that carries constraints | hidden **leading** parameters, one per constraint in canonical order, invisible in beni and fixed at every call site by the checker. A top-level declaration's are `$m$<k>`. **A generalised `let` function binding** (2026-09-27, the owner's decision that a constrained `let` function generalises: `checker-v2.md` Â§8.4, Â§13.1) takes them too, named `$l<inst>$<k>` after its `let_def` instruction so an inner binding never shadows an outer name it captures: `function inner($l2$0, a, b)`, or its `const` arrow for a `lambda` right-hand side; each use passes its evidence first, a reference in value position is the eta-expansion over the binding's arity, and a lambda inside reads the names by capture. A `let` value binding never takes evidence (the value restriction) |
| a derived `eq` / `compare` | a generated top-level function per type or per structural shape, emitted sorted by printed name |

The last five are static dispatch's, and
[`static-dispatch-spike.md`](static-dispatch-spike.md) Â§8 and Â§9 are the contract: Â§8 for the four
call shapes and the evidence convention, Â§9 for the exact JavaScript of every derived function.
Nothing here reopens a representation decision â Â§9.4's shapes are what derivation walks.

### Ordered dictionaries

*Added 2026-10-22 (#294), specifying the owner's 2026-10-17 and 2026-10-19
decisions; specified before implementation. This extends Â§4's table and
*Every platform edits in place* to Dict and Set. It supersedes tree-based
representation and iteration claims. `language.md` Â§6.8 owns the public API.*

`core/Dict` declares `pub equatable foreign type Dict k v`. Its JavaScript
value is `{ entries, index }`: `entries` is a dense array of private two-slot
arrays `[key, value]` in insertion order; `index` is a native `Map` from key to
the pair's zero-based position. The value is stored in the entry, never in the
Map. Each entry carries its key, so iteration reads `entries[i][0]` and
`entries[i][1]` without a Map lookup. Both fields and each entry pair are
private runtime storage, never a beni record, tuple or List exposed to callers.

The invariant is a bijection: `index.size === entries.length`, each key occurs
once, and `index.get(entries[i][0]) === i`. No tombstones, holes or parallel key
array exist. A lookup uses `Map.get`; distinguish absence with `position ===
undefined`, since zero is a valid position and a stored value can be `â¤`.
Keys are checked `Int` or `String`; native SameValueZero agrees with their
key identity (`-0` and `0` name one Int key). No key encoding, comparator,
object-property lookup or broad catch is involved. These Map operations have
no expected failure to catch (rule 9).

`insert` overwrites the entry's value when present, otherwise appends a new
pair and records its position. `remove` splices the pair and reindexes the
tail. `swap` exchanges two pairs and updates two index positions. `insertAt`
removes the previous occurrence before clamping and inserting, then reindexes
the affected tail. `sortBy` evaluates its callback once per entry in entry
order, stably sorts decorated entries by the supplied comparison evidence,
writes the permutation back and rebuilds the index. Temporaries used to sort
are algorithmic workspace, not a persistent or copying fallback. Callback
loops preserve the effects contract, including suspension; a native sort
comparator cannot call a suspendable beni callback. No half-updated collection
is handed to a callback.

Lookup, membership and size take expected O(1). Replacing an existing entry,
append insertion and swap take expected/amortised O(1). Removing and insert-at
take O(n); iteration, copying and rebuilding an index take O(n). Sorting takes
O(n log n), plus the callback's work. These are representation costs, not
measurements or claims about a browser benchmark.

Every accepted writer mutates this storage on every platform. Ownership is
required even when the dynamic operation does nothing. There is one writer,
with no persistent alternative or silent copy. `copy` allocates a new header,
entries array, entry pairs and Map, while retaining the values themselves.
This prevents replacing a value in one copy from changing another's pair.
`toList` also builds fresh beni tuples and a fresh List; `values` builds a fresh
List of the values, and neither exposes the private entries array or pairs.
`Set` stays an opaque wrapper over `Dict t â¤` and delegates its storage to it.

*Amended 2026-10-22, the owner's review of #664:* empty builders are ordinary
functions of `â¤`: `Dict.empty â¤` and `Set.empty â¤`, following
`Schema.defaultOptions`'s change of 2026-10-19. Each call allocates fresh
storage. There is no compiler special case for either name and no mutable
module-level singleton Map. An ordinary binding that stores a call's result
aliases that one constructed value; its later reads do not construct it again.
Passing `Dict.empty` or `Set.empty` as a function value follows the ordinary
calling convention and constructs fresh storage at each call too.

`eq` checks header identity first, then length and scalar keys and value `eq`
in one array walk. No `compare` is emitted or structurally derived for either
collection. In-place edits must never meet renderer identity comparisons of
the collection or entries (`browser-direct.md` Â§7.4), the same obligation as
for List. This work does not add keyed `For` or write-set positions (O3).

The sibling follows `boundary.md` Â§4's four checks: the foreign type has the
accepted shape, exports match declarations exactly, imports name declared
dependencies, and exported functions write countable parameter lists with
evidence parameters first. Higher-order loops may remain in beni over private
primitives; moving them to a synchronous host callback must not lose effects
or the declared ownership summaries (`ownership-checker.md` Â§32).

*Amended 2026-10-22 (#294, the owner's Tea decision):* the platform's job
and subscription tables are private sorted arrays of `(key, value)` pairs,
searched by binary search with `Hosted.compare`. Jobs use lexicographic
`List Hosted.Key` paths; subscription tables use `Hosted.Key`. They are
edited in place under ownership,
with no copying fallback. They are not Dicts and do not encode a key as an
Int or String: a type's own comparator can equate distinct representations.
`boundary.md` Â§9.8.3 specifies search, replacement, iteration and the contiguous
prefix range used by `cancelAll`. W47's type identities and comparison evidence
remain unchanged. Dict and Set themselves no longer have `compare` and are
refused as keys with the reason named in the diagnostic.

### Corrections to the representation

Three rows of that table did not survive contact with the code. Each is a
decision the implementation had to make and Â§4 did not:

1. **`Basics.Bool` is JavaScript's `true`/`false`.** Â§4 has no row for it and its general rule â
   a nullary constructor is the bare tag â would make `True` the string `"True"`, so `if` would
   compare strings and `&&` could not be `&&`. The special case is keyed on core's `Basics.Bool`,
   not on a name, so a user's own `type Bool = True | False` is an ordinary ADT.
2. **"Nullary constructor â the bare tag" and "padded to a uniform shape per type" cannot both
   hold**, and Â§9.4 states both. For `Maybe`, a bare `"Nothing"` beside `{$:"Just",a}` is exactly
   the shape inconsistency Â§9.4 measures 11% on Firefox for. The backend splits on the TYPE: a type whose
   constructors are *all* nullary is a bare tag string (`Order` is `"LT"`), and a type with any
   argument-taking constructor pads every constructor (`Nothing` is `{$:"Nothing",a:null}`).
3. **`&&` and `||` are lowered here, not at print time.** Â§9.4 files the primitive peephole under
   optimisation. For these two it is not one: `language.md` Â§6.5 desugars them into calls of
   `Basics.and`/`Basics.or`, a call evaluates both arguments, and `Basics.and` is `foreign`
   precisely so that it does not. A saturated call of either becomes `&&`/`||`, and when the right
   side needs statements of its own it becomes the `if`/`else` a short circuit really is.
   Arithmetic and comparison stay calls; that peephole really is the optimiser's (Â§9).
   *Amended 2026-10-02:* no optimiser took it, and arithmetic is an operator in both builds now â
   *Arithmetic is an operator*, below.

And one thing Â§4's table is silent on that the emitter had to settle: **where the empty list comes
from.** "cons cells (`{$:1, a, b}` / the empty singleton)" does not say who owns the singleton, and
it cannot be a sibling export because `boundary.md` Â§4's second check forbids a sibling from
exporting anything that is not a declared `foreign` value. The backend emits `{$:0,a:null,b:null}` inline,
and `core/List.js` and `core/String.js` build the same shape by contract. That contract is the one
piece of the representation that is written down in two places.

Two more rows the table did not state and the backend needed: a **`Char`** is a one-scalar JavaScript string
(Â§4 says strings are native and core's API exposes code points; a `Char` is the one-character case
of that), and **`()`** is `null` (under `--release`, `null` or `undefined`: *A `()` result is not written*). Neither is contentious; both are recorded because the table did
not say.

**Lists and strings are the two representation questions Â§14 left open.** The backend ships cons cells and
native strings, which are Elm's answers and the ones pattern matching and interop respectively push
toward. The optimiser benchmarks a 32-way persistent vector trie against cons cells on real idiomatic code, as
open question 2 requires, and records the result here either way.

*Amended 2026-10-01.* The benchmark was taken (research 38 Â§3âÂ§17, research 46) and the list half
is decided: *Lists are arrays*, below. The empty list then comes from nowhere in particular â it is
`[]` â and the paragraph above about its singleton being written down in two places is withdrawn
with the cons cell; what every file that reads a list shares instead is that subsection's
three-point protocol.

### A nullary constructor is one object

*Added 2026-09-29* (research 39 Â§10.3; decided by the project's manager on the owner's delegation).
Correction 2 above pads every constructor of a type that has any constructor with fields, so
`Nothing` is `{$: "Nothing", a: null}` â and until this amendment that literal was written at every
use, so `Run` in a `view` was a new object on every render. A helper call in a hole is skipped only
when its arguments are identical (`language.md` Â§11.6), so `button "run" Run` was called on every
render and never skipped, and `language.md` Â§11.12's identity promise bought nothing for the
commonest message there is. **A padded nullary constructor is now one module-level constant per
constructor, in the development build and under `--release` alike**: every use a module writes â
in value position, as a top-level value, as an argument, as a `==` operand that is not tested in
place, as a message in markup â reads the same `const`, so `Run` is `===` `Run` wherever that
module wrote it. Values are immutable, so sharing one is sound; nothing in beni can tell it from a
fresh one except a platform's reference check, which is the point.

- **Where it lives: the module that uses it**, in the synthesised run beside Â§9.1's comparators â
  `const <Module>$<Ctor> = {$: "<Ctor>", a: null, â¦};` for a constructor the module declares, and
  `<Module>$<Declaring$Module>$<Ctor>` for one it imports (`Main$Maybe$Nothing`). The constants are
  written in front of the markup hoists and the rest of the run, so a top-level `none = Nothing`
  reads an initialised `const`. The names cannot collide with a declaration (lower-case), a derived
  function (`$$`) or an import (`<Module>$<value>`), and `--release` renames them with every other
  top-level name (Â§9 item 2).
- **Written only when used.** Like the comparators the constant is *discovered* while a surviving
  body is lowered (Â§9), so an eliminated declaration's constructors write nothing, and a module that
  builds no padded nullary constructor does not move by a byte. A pattern, a tag test, `?`, and `==`
  tested in place (below) read the tag and never the constant.
- **Per module, not per program**, and deliberately. One object for the whole program would live in
  the declaring module, which a build would then have to write and import for one constant â a file
  for `core/Maybe` in every program that says `Nothing` â and core's siblings build their own
  `Nothing` anyway (`String.toInt`), so a program-wide identity could not be promised. What the
  render loop needs is narrower and holds: **the same expression yields the same object every time
  it runs**, and a value that is not rebuilt keeps its identity (`language.md` Â§11.12).
- **Not changed**: an all-nullary type is still its bare tag string, which has identity already;
  `Bool` is still `true`/`false`; the empty list is still built at each use (Â§4's list row, a
  separate representation); a record alias's constructor still builds its record.

*Amended 2026-10-24 (#916): one constant for the one file.* "Per module" was decided for files:
one object for the whole program would need a file to import it from. A release application is
one scope-hoisted file (§9), where there is no import to pay for, so there each imported
nullary constructor's constant is declared once. Each module that builds one still declares its
`<Module>$<Declaring$Module>$<Ctor>`; the link step (`Emit.shareNullaries`) keeps the first
declaration in the file's order and drops every later one, whose name is numbered as the first's.
The first is evaluated before every later module, and every one is the same object literal of
constants, so each use reads an equal value, and the render loop's rule above still holds: the
same expression yields the same object every time it runs. A constant of a module's own
constructor (`<Module>$<Ctor>`), a multi-file build and a development build are as before. On
S1 seed 1 this is one `{$:1,a:null}` in place of one per widget module: −2.6 B per widget from
N = 64 to 256 (`emit/release/app/NullaryShared`).

Fixtures: `emit/NullaryConstant` (local and imported constants, a top-level use, uses inside
functions), `run/NullaryIdentity/` (`refEq` through a test platform, dev and `--release`, as Â§15.8's),
`browser/dom/NullaryHelperSkip` (`button "run" Run` called once, at mount).
