#### The representation: a plain array (the owner, 2026-10-15)

*Added 2026-10-15; specified, not built. It is built by `browser-direct.md` Â§14's slice S7, as
amended the same day (`browser-direct.md`, the last amendment, *`List` is a plain array; S7
replaces its representation*), and until S7 lands the subsections after this one describe what
the compiler emits. Once it lands, this subsection is the representation and wins wherever the
text after it disagrees. Those subsections are kept as the record of E1t and E1tp as built.*

The owner's decision, 2026-10-15, verbatim: **"I want the trie gone from the bundle. It might be
included later as custom data structure (like Vector) if the developer want. List is regular
array."**

The ownership checker ([`ownership-checker.md`](ownership-checker.md)) exists so that a `List` can
be a plain JavaScript array edited in place. Without it, the persistent list (E1tp) would be the
right representation, and it would stay. With it, the trie only keeps lists persistent, and
the checker already proves that no program on an in-place platform reads an old version after a
write. So the trie is withdrawn. It is not kept as a fallback for when that proof is missing.

**The forms.** A `List` value is one of two forms. The trie is gone:

| Form | JavaScript | Which lists have it |
|---|---|---|
| **plain** | a JavaScript array; the elements are `a[0] â¦ a[a.length â 1]` | every list except a view: `[]`, a literal, every result that builds, every result of a writer, a decoder's result, a sibling's result |
| **view** | `{ $b, $o, length }`: the elements `$b[$o] â¦ $b[$b.length â 1]` of a plain array `$b`, a suffix, `1 â¤ $o`, `length === $b.length â $o`, never empty | what a pattern's `rest` binds outside a scalarised loop, `List.tail`, `List.drop`. **Read-only**: nothing writes through a view (below) |

A view is the one form that is not an array, and it is kept for one reason: **recursion over a
list's suffix stays O(n).** Â§8's *Scalar views* turns a *tail-recursive* `[ x, â¦rest ]` walk into
an index loop with no view at all. But a walk that is not one of those loops still needs an O(1)
`rest`. That covers non-tail recursion (`x + sum rest`), mutual recursion, a `rest` passed to
another function or returned, a `rest` captured by a closure, a `List.tail` and a `List.drop`.
Without a view, each of those steps copies the suffix. A walk of n elements then copies
n â 1 + n â 2 + â¦ elements: **O(nÂ²)** where the cons list and E1tp were O(n). A view is three
fields and no code a writer needs, so it keeps every such walk linear for a few dozen bytes. A
`rest` that is never read whole costs nothing; Â§7 already binds no unread tail.

The view's keys begin with `$`, so no beni record can have them (a field name is a lower-case
identifier). That is how `Debug.toString` and the protocol tell a view from a record:
`Array.isArray(v) || v.$b !== undefined` is "v is a list". A host object with a `$b` key never
holds a position typed `List`, because a sibling returns a list only as a fresh plain array
(`boundary.md` Â§4). The one reader that could still meet such an object is `Debug.toString`,
called on a value of a `foreign` type. S7 states how `Debug` prints a value of a `foreign` type
before it changes the test, and pins that with a fixture: a host object with a `$b` key, printed. The old view's cached `p` and its
`$plain` method go, and so do `Js.method`'s two uses in `core/List`.

**Writes.** The writers are `set`, `update`, `swap`, `push`, `pop`, `insertAt`, `removeAt`,
`List.append`, and every construction with something after its first spread (`[ â¦xs, x ]`,
`[ â¦a, â¦b ]`, a `++` chain on lists; `ownership-checker.md` Â§3.1âÂ§3.2). Each one is a **demand**,
and what it does depends on the platform:

- **On an in-place platform** (`"lists": "in-place"`, `ownership-checker.md` Â§28.2), every demand
  in a program that builds is one the checker accepted. Any other demand is already a compile
  error: `list_still_used`, `top_level_list_changed`, `view_changes_model` or
  `list_may_be_shared` (Â§28.5). An accepted demand **edits its base's array in place and returns
  that array**:
  - `set`/`update`: `a[i] = v`.
  - `swap`: two stores.
  - `push`: `a.push(v)`.
  - `pop`: `a.pop()`.
  - `insertAt`/`removeAt`: one `splice`.
  - a construction: the base extended from left to right, by `ownership-checker.md` Â§3.3's order.
    The items are evaluated first, then the base is written. Items before the base
    (`[ x, â¦xs, y ]`) go in front of it.

  There is no reference count, no run-time ownership test, and no copy the program did not write
  (research 42's R0, taken statically). **An unsafe edit is never turned into a silent copy**:
  the owner's standing rule, `ownership-checker.md` Â§28.1. Where a program needs an old version,
  it writes `List.copy`, O(n), and the checker's message offers exactly that fix.
- **On any other platform**, the checker does not run (Â§28.3), so no write can be proved
  unshared. Every writer and every construction **copies its base and writes the copy**: O(n)
  per write, where E1tp was amortised O(1) or O(logââ n). *This is the open question below.*

**A view is never written.** A demand whose base is a view first makes a plain array of the
view's elements, O(length of the view), and then writes it as above. This is not a
sharing fallback. On an in-place platform the checker has already proved that nothing else
reads the list; the copy is only the price of a form that has no room of its own. A
`List.push rest y` on the `rest` of a match therefore costs O(n). The queue idiom (push at the
end, match at the front), which E1tp's prefix removal kept amortised O(1), is O(n) a step (the
cost table in `language.md` Â§6.8). Writing through a view would make it amortised O(1) again:
the view is a suffix, so its end is its base's end. That is sound by the same ownership argument,
because a pattern's `rest` aliases its scrutinee's cells (`ownership-checker.md` Â§4). But it rests
on view aliasing, which the Lean oracle does not yet model (`browser-direct.md`'s S7 condition C2).
So it is not part of this amendment. It can be added later on its own measurement.

**A prepend copies**, as decided on 2026-10-11 (*The claimable head: E1tp*, amended):
`[ x, â¦xs ]` and `List.cons` make a fresh array, O(length of `xs`). A prepend is not a demand
(`ownership-checker.md` Â§25.2), so it is the same on every platform. The re-cons of a view
(`b[o â 1] === x` gives the view at `o â 1`, or `b` itself) stays. It reads `b[o â 1]`, which is
outside the view, so it is sound only while `b` is unwritten since the view was made. Invariant 3
and the checker give exactly that: the view aliases `b`'s cells, so a write to `b` while the view
is still read is `list_still_used`. S7's fixtures include a re-cons after a `List.copy` of the
base was written. That write must not reach the view. The trie's re-cons row goes
with the trie.

**Invariants**, replacing *Invariants* below; the numbering is kept so references still hold:

1. **A published array is written only at an accepted demand on an in-place platform**, and only
   through the list that demand names. Nothing else writes a published array: not a sibling, not a
   platform runtime, not the markup runtime, not `Debug`, not the derived-comparison engine. On
   a platform that is not in-place, nothing published is ever written. A demand never extends an
   array past its end except through `push`, `insertAt` at `length`, or a construction: an
   out-of-range `set`, `update`, `swap`, `insertAt` or `removeAt` returns its input unchanged,
   and `pop` of `[]` returns `[]`. The old claim and cache exceptions go with the trie.
2. *Withdrawn with the trie.*
3. **A view's backing array is plain**, and while a view of it is live, nothing writes it. The
   checker guarantees this: a pattern's `rest`, `tail` and `drop` alias their list's cells, so a
   write to the base while the view is read later is `list_still_used`.
4. **The empty list is plain.** No view is empty.
5. **A builder is owned** (unchanged).
6. **Elements are references** (unchanged).
7. **A list literal is a fresh array at every evaluation** wherever a demand can reach it. This
   covers `[]`, `[ a, b ]` and every core value that is an empty list. No pass of the emitter,
   Â§9's optimiser or `Minify` may hoist, intern or share a constant array literal across
   evaluations. If one did, one call's in-place write would become every later call's state, and
   the checker cannot see it: `top_level_list_changed` covers the program's own top-level values,
   not a literal the emitter hoists. S7 adds an `emit/release/` fixture that pins this.
8. **No runtime retains a list across a message on an in-place platform.** This covers a platform
   runtime, the markup runtime, `Debug` and a sibling. A view's `length` is a snapshot, and a
   later accepted demand may write the array behind a plain list. A runtime that needs a list
   past the call that handed it over says so in its ownership words (`ownership-checker.md` Â§24),
   so the checker counts the retention as a holder. A runtime that compares a retained list by
   identity is the case `browser`'s `For` skip is (the open question below).

**The reader protocol**, replacing *What a reader of a list may rely on* below. A reader outside
`core/List` may rely on these:

1. **`xs.length`** is the number of elements, in both forms.
2. **`Array.isArray(xs)`** is true exactly for the plain form, whose elements are
   `xs[0 â¦ length â 1]`.
3. Otherwise `xs` is a view, and its elements are **`xs.$b[xs.$o + i]`** for `0 â¤ i < length`.
   A reader indexes it in place. If a reader needs an array of its own, `xs.$b.slice(xs.$o)` is
   that array. It is the reader's copy, and `core/List` does not cache it.

The idiom is `const a = Array.isArray(xs) ? xs : xs.$b, o = Array.isArray(xs) ? 0 : xs.$o;`,
then an index loop from `o`. `$plain()` is withdrawn. No reader may write either form (invariant
1). What a sibling may return as a list is unchanged: a fresh plain array, or a list it was
given.

**The runtime.** `core/List` keeps:

- `cons`;
- `append` and `concat`, which build fresh arrays;
- the readers;
- `view`, `base` and `offset`: `base`/`offset` of a plain list are `(xs, 0)` and of a view
  `($b, $o)`;
- `unsafeGet`, which is O(1) in both forms;
- the builder;
- the in-place writers, which are core-private and which the emitter names at an accepted demand
  by well-known symbol, as it names `List.cons`;
- the copying writers, which are the public functions on a platform that is not in-place.

It loses every `trie*` function, `fromPlain`, the tree and header shapes, `triePlain`,
`viewPlain`, the two thresholds and every reader's form test for a trie. **Nothing of the trie
is in any bundle.** Research 102 Â§2 priced that part at 672 B brotli on `browser-tea`'s Conduit
and 565 B on `browser-direct`'s. Research 87's direct table app paid 594 B, leave-one-out, for
*List representation, append and indexed get*. The trie is most of that.
`bench/arrays/lists/claim-test.mjs` and `claim-prepend-test.mjs` test the trie's claims and
retire with it. `run/ListForms` and `browser/dom/ForForms` lose their trie inputs and keep their
view inputs.

**Identity.** On an in-place platform a writer returns **its input array itself**, edited. So
a written list is the same object as before. Nobody can observe that, because the checker has
proved that no holder of the old list reads it again. W27's amendment for in-place update
(`browser-direct.md` Â§15, Q4, decided 2026-10-09; `language.md` Â§11.12 still has to be written)
says the same for lists. On any other platform, a writer that writes returns a fresh array. Both
kinds of platform keep the promises that stay in *Identity* below: the input itself when there is
nothing to write, element identity, a view the same list as another view at the same offset. The
trie-header bullets of that section are withdrawn.

**`--release`.** The read/write split now has nothing to split: no write code is larger than a
store or a `push`. The demand is a **barrier** to Â§9's optimiser (thesis Â§9.6, A5). Item 1 may
not move a read of the base, or of anything that aliases it, across the demand. It may not
inline a single-use binding of the old list past it either, and it may not drop the demand as
an unused pure call. The demand's result is the same array, so dropping the call would lose the
write.

**What is not done.**

- **No persistent structure behind `List`.** The trie and anything like it (RRB, a finger tree,
  a fat array with version stamps) may return only as a **separate type the developer chooses**,
  such as a `Vector`, with its own module, its own costs and no implicit conversion. It is never
  `List`'s representation and never a fallback the compiler picks. Whether core or a package
  ships one is a later decision. The owner's sentence above is its whole scope.
- **No run-time ownership.** Research 42's reference counts are still not taken: ownership is
  static or it is a compile error.
- **No write through a view**, yet (above).

**Open, the owner's: what a write costs where lists are not edited in place.** Today only
`browser-direct` declares `"lists": "in-place"`. `browser-tea`, `browser`, `html`, `node` and the
test platforms do not, so with no trie every write there copies its base. Concretely:

- A loop that builds a list with `List.push` or `[ â¦acc, x ]` is **O(nÂ²)** there.
  At 10 000 elements it copies about 50 million element references. E1tp did the same build in
  amortised O(1) per element.
- A `List.set` on a long list is O(n) where it was O(logââ n).
- `node` is the platform every `run/` fixture runs on. A fixture that builds a few thousand
  elements by pushing could go over the 4 300-million-instruction test budget (CLAUDE.md,
  *Building*) for a cost the browser never pays.

There are two ways to answer this, and they cost different things.

- **(a) Edit in place everywhere.** Make the property the language's rule, not a platform's: the
  checker runs in every `check` and `build`, and every platform lowers an accepted demand in
  place. Every list then costs the same everywhere, and the harness measures what the browser
  runs. The price:
  - Every program on every platform must pass the checker. How many corpus and `node` programs
    fail today is unmeasured. `dump --stage=ownership` over the whole corpus, under each platform
    (a) would cover, is a **hard precondition** of choosing (a). A fixture that fails would force
    a choice between rewriting the fixture and bending the design, and that choice is the owner's
    under CLAUDE.md rule 10, made on the measured list, not discovered during S7.
  - `browser`'s markup runtime, which `browser-tea` is layered on, skips a `For` whose list is
    `===` the last one rendered (Â§15.5, *Identity*). An in-place write keeps that identity, so the
    skip would show a stale page. That runtime must stop deciding "unchanged" by a list's
    identity before an in-place write reaches it. This is `browser-direct.md` Â§7.4's first rule,
    which direct already keeps.
  - The entry rows of `ownership-checker.md` Â§20.2 must exist for each platform's program
    constructors.
- **(b) Copy where nothing is proved.** Keep in-place a platform property, and accept O(n) copies
  on `browser-tea` until S8 retires it, and on `node`. A `browser-tea` list is the size of a UI,
  and its renderer already walks it, so O(n) per message changes its order of cost only for
  programs that build long lists in a loop. `node`, though, would run quadratic builds that the
  browser does not.

*Recommendation:* **(a) for `node`, `html` and the test platforms, landed with S7, so that no
platform the gates run ever runs the quadratic build; (b) for `browser-tea` and `browser` until
S8.** If S8 keeps `browser-direct`, the question closes with `browser-tea`'s deletion. If it keeps
`browser-tea` instead, (a) applies to it too, once its identity skips are removed. This is not
decided here. The owner decides it before S7's lowering lands, because it decides which platforms
the copying writers serve.

*Answered 2026-10-15 by the owner: (a), on every platform, and (b) nowhere. The next subsection,
*Every platform edits in place*, is the answer.*

#### Every platform edits in place (the owner, 2026-10-15)

*Added 2026-10-15; specified, not built. It is built by the slices of `ownership-checker.md` Â§30.
It closes the open question above. Wherever *The representation: a plain array* says "on an
in-place platform", read "on every platform". Its "On any other platform" bullet under *Writes*,
the copying writers under *The runtime*, and the "any other platform" column of `language.md`
Â§6.8's cost table are withdrawn.*

The owner's decision, 2026-10-15, verbatim: **"no 'fallbacks', i want a proper implementation.
this is no longer a platform decision, it's core to beni."**

**The rule is the language's.** Ownership is no longer a property a platform declares. The
ownership checker runs in every `check` and every `build`: on `node`, `html`, `browser`,
`browser-tea`, `browser-direct`, every test platform, every platform a third party writes, and
with no platform at all. On every platform, every demand in a program that builds is one the
checker accepted, and the emitter lowers it in place. Every other demand is a compile error
(`ownership-checker.md` Â§28.5). The manifest key `"lists"` is withdrawn (`boundary.md` Â§5.2,
amended). So one list program costs the same on every platform, and the `run/` corpus on `node`
measures the code a browser runs.

**There is no fallback anywhere.** None of these exist, on any platform:

- a copy where ownership is not proved;
- a copying writer beside the in-place one;
- a `"lists"`-gated lowering;
- a trie, or any other persistent structure behind `List`;
- an interim in which constructions copy over plain arrays.

A program that needs an old version writes `List.copy`, and the checker's message offers it. The
O(n) copies that remain are the ones a program asks for by what it writes. Each is the same on
every platform:

- `List.copy`;
- a prepend, which copies (decided 2026-10-11) and is not a demand;
- a write whose base is a view, which first makes the view plain. That copy is about the view's
  form, not about sharing (*The representation: a plain array*);
- the functions that build a new list (`map`, `filter`, `concat`, the sorts and the rest).

**One set of writers.** `core/List`'s public `set`, `update`, `swap`, `push`, `pop`, `insertAt`,
`removeAt` and `append` are the in-place writers. No copying twin exists for a platform or for
a value. A writer handed to a function as a value is the same function. Every call through it
is a demand the checker decides, or the checker rejects the value where it leaves its sight
(`ownership-checker.md` Â§30.4). So no call writes in place unchecked, and none copies silently.

**In-place constructions land with the trie's removal.** Without a trie, a copying
`[ â¦acc, x ]` makes every building loop O(nÂ²). So no build of beni lowers lists as plain arrays
while it still lowers constructions by copying. The representation, the in-place lowering of
every demand and the removal of the trie are one slice (`ownership-checker.md` Â§30.5, O5). That
slice comes after the oracle's conditions C1âC5 (`browser-direct.md`, the last amendment).

**What every runtime keeps, on every platform.** Invariants 1, 3 and 8 above now hold on every
platform.

- **No runtime writes a list.** This covers a platform runtime, a sibling, the markup runtime,
  `Debug` and the derived-comparison engine.
- **No runtime keeps a list across a message unless its words say so.** A runtime that keeps a
  list past the call that handed it over must say so in its ownership words, and the default
  for a `foreign` with no words is `escaped` (`ownership-checker.md` Â§24.5).
- **No runtime decides "unchanged" from a list's identity.** It may not skip work because a
  list, or a value that a release build represents by a list, is `===` the one it saw last, or
  is a view over the same base at the same offset. Â§15.5, amended the same day, says what that
  removes from the `dom` lowering's runtime and what the change costs.

The identity of every value that is not a list still means "unchanged", as `language.md` Â§11.12
promises. The reason is that only lists are written in place. `browser-direct.md` Â§7.4's
assignment to records waits on its own condition C4. Until C4 lands, a record, a tuple, a
constructor or a closure that is `===` the one seen last was not rebuilt, so it holds the same
lists. The checker also proves that a list was not written in place while anything that holds
it is read afterwards (thesis P7, *Why write sets provide it*).

**Identity of a written list.** On every platform, a writer that writes returns its input
array, edited. The *Identity* bullets about a fresh array "on any other platform" are
withdrawn.

*Amended 2026-10-17 (the owner; `ownership-checker.md` Â§31; specified, not built):* **records are
written in place on every platform too.** A record update consumes its base (`language.md` Â§6.3, amended).
The paragraph above that keeps a record's identity as "unchanged" until C4 lands is withdrawn: C4 is
superseded by `ownership-checker.md` Â§31. The table's *record* row keeps its literal, and a record update is
no longer the spread `({ ...r, a: x })`:

- **Lowering** (`ownership-checker.md` Â§31.10): the base into a temporary `b`, each new value into a
  temporary in written order, then `b.a = tâ; â¦`, and the update's value is `b`. Every value is evaluated
  before any field is written. A store keeps the object's hidden class, and under `--release` it uses the
  field's short name (Â§9, *Item 4, taken up*).
- **No choice is made at a site.** A module reaches lowering only when the ownership pass accepted every
  demand in it, so every record update is lowered in place. There is no spread path to fall back to.
- **Hoists** (*revised the same day*, `ownership-checker.md` Â§31.14). A later read of a written field is read
  into a temporary before the write, at the placement the checker's table names, and a closure that captures a
  field path reads it when it is made. The table is in the module's cache entry beside its summary block
  (`ownership-checker.md` Â§31.10).
- **A barrier.** A record update is a barrier to Â§9's optimiser, as a list demand is (*`--release`*, above).
  No read of a written field, or of anything that may alias the base, is moved across it. No single-use
  binding of such a read is inlined past it. It is never dropped as unused.
- **Invariant 8 for records.** No runtime concludes "unchanged" from the identity of a value that may hold a
  record (Â§15.5, amended the same day). A runtime may keep such a value, but it never reads it expecting the
  contents it had.

*As built 2026-10-23 (#315, R6; `ownership-checker.md` §31.12 slice 3):* the lowering above, in every module
whose table is clean — an application module checked under enforcement, every demand accepted. Core, the
platforms and any module checked without enforcement keep `({ ...r, a: x })` until O4, so their output did not
move. `--sanitize-records` (hidden, development only) is the stale-read sanitiser for records.

#### The representation: E1t

*Superseded 2026-10-15 by *The representation: a plain array* (above), once S7 lands; kept as the record.*

The representation is the one research 38 Â§17.2 calls **E1t**: *E1* â Â§16's adaptive array, a plain
JavaScript array until something writes to it, plus the O(1) view an `x :: rest` pattern makes â
with a claimable **t**ail on its trie. A `List` value is one of three **forms**:

| Form | JavaScript | Which lists have it |
|---|---|---|
| **plain** | a JavaScript array; the elements are `a[0] â¦ a[a.length â 1]` | every list nothing has written: `[]`, a literal, and the result of every operation that builds a fresh sequence â `map`, `filter`, `range`, `initialize`, `slice`, `reverse`, the sorts, `concat`, `::`, `++`, `insertAt`, `removeAt`, a decoder, a sibling â and a list written below the thresholds. *E1tp:* `::` (`[ x, ...xs ]`) only onto a list of fewer than 32 elements. *Amended 2026-10-11:* `[ x, â¦xs ]` onto any list, as under E1t, except a runtime re-cons (*The claimable head: E1tp*, amended) |
| **view** | `{ b, o, length, $plain }`: the elements `b[o] â¦ b[b.length â 1]` of a plain array `b` | what an `x :: rest` pattern binds as `rest`, `List.tail`, `List.drop`. Never empty, `o â¥ 1`, `length === b.length â o`: a view is always a **suffix** of its backing array. *E1tp:* only of a plain list or a view; those of a trie are tries |
| **trie** | `{ length, s, r, t, p, $plain }`: the Clojure and Elm 32-way persistent vector â a root `r` whose height is the shift `s` (a multiple of 5), leaves of exactly 32 elements, and a **tail** array `t` holding the last 1 to 32 elements; `p` is the cached plain copy, or `null`. *E1tp:* `{ length, h, hc, T, t, p, $plain }`, with a claimable head `h` and the tree `T = { r, s, off, tc }` at a radix offset (*The claimable head: E1tp*, below) | the result of a single-element write (`set`, `update`, `swap`, `push`, `pop`) to a plain list above its threshold, and every write to a trie. *E1tp:* also a prepend onto a list of 32 or more, and a trie without its first elements (`rest`, `tail`, `drop`) unless only tail elements are left. *Amended 2026-10-11:* no prepend makes or keeps a trie; the prefix removal still does |

**The thresholds.** `push` converts a plain list of **32** elements or more to a trie; `set`,
`update`, `swap` and `pop` convert one longer than **256**. Below them a write is copy-on-write and
the result is plain. The two numbers are research 38 Â§15.11 and Â§17.2's, they are constants of
`core/List.js`, and a change to either is a measurement's to make, on research 38 Â§15's and Â§17's
scenarios through `bench/arrays`. A read-mostly UI list of up to 256 rows therefore stays plain through `set`, and a list
built by `push` stops copying at 32.

**The representation is not canonical.** The same elements may be any of the three forms, and no
result a beni program can compute depends on which: `==`, `compare`, `Debug.toString`, every
function of `core/List`, every sibling and every platform runtime accept all three. Only speed, and
the identities of *Identity* below, can tell them apart.

#### The claimable head: E1tp

*Superseded 2026-10-15 by *The representation: a plain array* (above), once S7 lands; kept as the record.*

*Added 2026-10-01, the owner's E1tp amendment of W35* (research 46 Â§11; the prototype is
`bench/arrays/ports/first-tail-prepend.js`). Under E1t, `[ x, ...xs ]` copied `xs`, so Elm-shaped
code that builds at the front â an accumulator then `List.reverse`, `foldr` building a list, a
persistent stack, paths that share their tails, a TEA list that gains rows at the top â was
quadratic: 11â2 500Ã the cons list at 10 000 elements on research 46 Â§11.4's table A. **E1tp** gives
the trie a second claimable buffer at its front, after Scala 2.13's `Vector` but without its
per-level prefix arrays: one header shape and a **radix offset**. The plain and view forms, the
thresholds and everything this subsection does not name are E1t's, unchanged.

*Amended 2026-10-11, the owner:* **the head is no longer claimable, and a prepend copies.**
Prepending is an anti-pattern the language must not reward â the cons list's habit of building at
the front and reversing â and on an array the natural build is a push at the end. A claimable head
made the habit cheap and so taught it (Â§8, *Accumulators build a plain array â withdrawn*, the
same argument). So **the representation reserves no room in front**:

- **`cons(x, xs)`** â what `[ x, â¦xs ]` and `List.cons` lower to â is a fresh plain array, `x`
  then the elements of `xs`, O(length of `xs`), onto every form, as under E1t. It never claims a
  head, never moves a full head into the tree, never grows the root left, and never converts a
  plain list or a view to a trie. The *Prepending* table below is withdrawn but for its two
  **re-cons** rows, which build nothing and stay: onto a view `(b, o)` with `b[o â 1] === x`, the
  view `(b, o â 1)` or `b` itself; onto a trie whose head array holds `x` in the slot past this
  version's count (`hc < h.length` and `h[hc] === x` â the tail of a trie that began with `x`), a
  header with `hc + 1` sharing every array. A loop that builds from fresh elements reaches
  neither, so neither rewards a prepend; both keep `pairwise` and a re-consing `merge` linear
  outside the scalar views of Â§8 (Â§7, *re-consing*).
- **What stays is the prefix removal** (*Removing a prefix*, below), unchanged: `view` of a trie â
  a pattern's `rest`, `List.tail`, `List.drop` â is a trie that shares the tree, O(1) and at most
  31 copied, never a flatten. It is not prepend machinery: it is what keeps a list pushed at one
  end and taken from the other (a queue) amortised O(1) a step, where E1t's view over the cached
  plain copy made each step after a push an O(n) flatten and an O(n) conversion back. So a trie
  keeps its `h`, `hc` and the tree's radix offset, and the **head is now only what a prefix
  removal leaves of the tree's first leaf**: a reversed fresh copy of at most 32, written once when
  it is made and never after. A trie that `push` or a conversion makes has an empty head and its
  tree at `off = 0`, and `off` only ever moves right. The reversed layout is kept because a
  further removal inside the head shares it (`hc â k`), exactly as before.
- **Invariant 1's head claim is withdrawn** (the exceptions are two again), and invariant 2's
  remark on the head holds as written: the head is never a leaf and never written.
- **What it costs.** Building by prepending is O(nÂ²) again â 11â2 500Ã the cons list at 10 000
  elements on research 46 Â§11.4's table A, E1t's figures â and the warning `prepend_in_loop`
  ([`checker-v2.md`](checker-v2.md) Â§35) is at the loops that do it, with the push form as the
  rewrite. Everything else costs what it did: `push`, `pop`, `set`, reads, walks and the prefix
  removal are untouched, and `cons` becomes a reader (*`--release`*, below), so a program that
  prepends and never pushes or sets ships none of the trie's write half.

The rest of this subsection is the record of E1tp as built on 2026-10-01; where it describes a
prepend onto a trie, the head claim, left growth or a conversion by `cons`, the amendment above
replaces it.

**The trie.** A header is `{ length, h, hc, T, t, p, $plain }`:

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `length` | the number of elements, a data field as on the other two forms |
| `h`, `hc` | the **head**: the first `hc` elements, `0 â¤ hc â¤ 32`, stored **reversed** â element `i < hc` is `h[hc â 1 â i]` â so that a prepend is an append to `h`, claimed as `push` claims the tail |
| `T` | the **tree**, `{ r, s, off, tc }`: `tc` elements at radix positions `off â¦ off + tc â 1` of the root `r`, whose shift is `s`; element `j` of the tree is `r[(off + j) >>> s & 31] â¦ [(off + j) & 31]`. `off` and `tc` are multiples of 32, so the tree is whole leaves and only where it starts moves. `T` is an object of its own, shared by every header between two changes to the tree â a prepend or a push that stays in its buffer, a tail inside the head, a `pop` inside the tail â so a list operation allocates a header of seven fields and not the tree |
| `t` | E1t's **tail**: the last `length â hc â tc` elements, 1 to 32, never empty |
| `p`, `$plain` | E1t's: the cached plain copy or `null`, and the protocol's function |

Element `i` is `h[hc â 1 â i]` for `i < hc`, the tree's element `i â hc` for `i < hc + tc`, and
`t[i â hc â tc]` after it: one comparison more than E1t in front of the same O(logââ n) descent and
no size table (research 46 Â§11.4 table C: `get` 5.1 ns against E1t's 5.3). A trie is never empty,
and `length > hc + tc` always.

**Prepending**, `cons(x, xs)`, which `[ x, ...xs ]` lowers to:

| Onto | Result | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| a trie with `hc < 32` and `h.length === hc` | **the head claim**: `x` is appended to `h` in place and a new header shares `h`, `T` and `t` | O(1) |
| a trie with `hc < 32` and `h[hc] === x` | the slot past this version's head already holds `x` â the version is the tail of one that began with `x` â so a new header with `hc + 1`, nothing written | O(1) | O(1) |
| any other trie with `hc < 32` | a copy of the `hc` head elements this version owns, then `x` | at most 32 |
| a trie with `hc === 32` | the head is reversed into a **fresh** leaf at radix `off â 32` (a path copy), `off` moves left by 32, and the head becomes `[x]`. When `off < 32` the root first **grows left**: a new root holding sixteen `null`s and then the old root, so the old root is child 16 and `off` moves right by sixteen of its spans; an empty tree starts at `off = 512`, mid-root, with room on both sides. `null` fills every gap left of a child, so every node stays a packed array | O(logââ n), once every 32 prepends |
| a plain list or a view of fewer than 32 elements | a fresh plain array, as under E1t | at most 32 |
| a plain list or a view of 32 or more | converted to a trie once â E1t's layout, a fresh empty head, the tree at `off = 0` â and prepended onto; every later prepend onto it or a version made from it is one of the rows above | O(n), once per plain list |
| a view `(b, o)` with `b[o â 1] === x`, tested before the two rows above | **the runtime re-cons**: the view `(b, o â 1)`, or `b` itself when `o = 1`; nothing copied | O(1) |

So a prepend is **amortised O(1) onto the newest version**, a copy of at most 31 elements onto an
older one, and O(n) at most once per plain list it converts.

**Removing a prefix.** `view(xs, k)` of a trie â a pattern's `rest`, `List.tail`, `List.drop` â is
a trie sharing the tree, never a flatten:

- `k â¤ hc`: a header with `hc â k`, sharing `h`, `T` and `t`.
- otherwise `kâ² = k â hc` more elements leave the tree's front. With `kâ² < tc`, `âkâ²/32â` whole
  leaves go by moving `off` right and `tc` down by 32 each, the nodes untouched; then, if
  `kâ² mod 32` is not 0, the rest of the new first leaf becomes the head â a reversed **fresh** copy
  of at most 31 â and `off` and `tc` move one leaf more. (The prototype writes `k = 1`; general `k`
  is the same rule, Scala's drop by offset.)
- with `kâ² â¥ tc`, only tail elements are left: a fresh plain array of at most 32, or `[]`.

That is O(1) and a copy of at most 31 elements â once every 32 steps of a walk. E1t made the tail
of a trie a view over the trie's cached plain copy, O(1) after an O(n) flatten but O(n) again to
prepend onto, which is exactly what a persistent stack does after a pop (research 46 Â§11.4,
*undo stack*: 41.3 ms â 429 Âµs).

**Everything else** is E1t's: `push` claims the tail, whose full array moves into the tree as the
leaf at radix `off + tc`, the root growing right; `pop` shares the tail, or makes the tree's last
leaf the tail, or â with no tree left â returns the head reversed as a fresh plain array, and it
collapses a root left with one live child; `set` copies the head, the tail or the path its index
falls in; `slice` and every bulk operation read through the cached plain copy and return plain
arrays.

**The radix positions are unsigned 32-bit.** The descent uses `>>>`, so every position stays below
2Â³Â². Pushes alone would reach it only past 2Â³Â² elements, more than a JavaScript array can hold; left
growth centres the old root, so one lineage reaches it after roughly 2Â²â¹ prepends â some 4 GB of
element references, beyond any browser tab's heap. `core/List.js` states the bound in a comment and
carries no check.

**What it costs and buys** (research 46 Â§11.4âÂ§11.6, Node, one round at 10 000 elements). Every
Elm-style row that was quadratic under E1t is linear: `x :: acc` then `reverse` 42.1 ms â 547 Âµs,
kept paths 423 ms â 1.16 ms, `foldr` building a list 55.5 ms â 526 Âµs, a TEA `Remove` 24.5 ms â
555 Âµs. Elm-style code still runs at 3â7Ã the cons list, so building with `push` stays the idiom to
teach. Array-first code costs what it cost under E1t within the batch's noise, except pushes at up
to about 1.3Ã (the extra indirection of `T`) and the merge sort of sorted input at about 2Ã (a
header per tail of a trie where E1t made a view over its cached copy; Â§8's *Scalar views* removes
both). The sibling grows by **429 bytes brotli**, 3 468 â 3 897 on the whole surface.

#### Invariants

*Superseded 2026-10-15 by *The representation: a plain array* (above), once S7 lands; kept as the record.*

Every piece of JavaScript that touches a list â `core/List.js`, the emitted code, a sibling, a
platform runtime, the derived-comparison engine â keeps these. A list is **published** from the
moment any code other than the operation creating it can reach it.

1. **Nothing published is written**, with exactly two exceptions, both invisible to every reader:
   - **The claim.** A trie's tail array `t` may be written at index `c`, this version's tail count
     (`length` minus the offset of its tail), **only when `t.length === c` and `c < 32`**: `push`
     onto the version that owns the end of `t` appends in place and returns a new header sharing
     the array. Every other version sharing `t` reads only its own first `câ² â¤ c` elements, so none
     can see the write. `push` onto any other version copies the at most 31 elements its tail owns
     first â never the whole list â and `pop` returns a header sharing `t`. This is Go's `append`
     made persistent by each version's own length (research 38 Â§17.2); it needs no analysis, and
     `bench/arrays/lists/claim-test.mjs` checked it 2.39 million times on randomly chosen old
     versions two levels deep.
   - **The cache.** A trie header's `p` is written once, from `null` to a fresh plain array holding
     its elements, the first time a walk, a `$plain()` or a bulk operation needs one. A view may
     cache its own `$plain()` the same way. It is derived data.
   - **The head claim** (*amended 2026-10-01, E1tp*: the exceptions are three; *withdrawn
     2026-10-11*: the head is written only by the fresh copy that makes it, and the exceptions are
     two again â *The claimable head: E1tp*, amended). A trie's head array
     `h` may be written at index `hc`, this version's head count, **only when `h.length === hc` and
     `hc < 32`**: a prepend onto the version that owns the end of `h` appends in place and returns a
     new header sharing it. It is the tail claim mirrored, and it is invisible for the same reason:
     every header's `hc` is at most `h.length`, and every other version sharing `h` reads only its
     own first `hcâ² â¤ hc` slots. A slot of `h` is therefore written **at most once**, which is what
     makes the prepend that finds `h[hc] === x` already there sound without writing. A prepend onto
     any other version copies at most 31 elements, and a tail inside the head shares `h`.
     `bench/arrays/lists/claim-prepend-test.mjs` checked the two claims together 3.04 million
     times on randomly chosen old versions, through two left growths of the root.
2. **A trie's tail is never a plain list's array, and never a leaf while it can be claimed.**
   Converting a plain list copies it (the tail too, so a claim never writes into an array some
   plain list is). A full tail of 32 moves into the tree as a leaf unchanged, and no version can
   claim it after: a claim needs `c < 32`, and a leaf is 32 long. No leaf and no inner node is
   written after the header that first published it. *Amended 2026-10-01 (E1tp):* **the same holds
   for the head, which is never a leaf at all.** A conversion starts a fresh empty head; a full head
   becomes a leaf only as a reversed *copy*; a head made from the tree's first leaf (removing a
   prefix) is a reversed fresh copy of at most 31. A leaf can become a **tail** â `pop` makes the
   tree's last leaf the tail â and is still never written, because it is 32 long and a claim needs
   `c < 32`. Left growth writes a new root and never the old one.
3. **A view's backing array is plain.** The tail of a trie is a view over its cached plain copy.
   *Amended 2026-10-01 (E1tp):* the tail of a trie is a trie, or a fresh plain array when only
   tail elements are left (*The claimable head: E1tp*); a view is made only of a plain list or a
   view, and its backing array is still plain.
4. **The empty list is plain.** No view and no trie is empty: `view` at the end, `pop` of the last
   element and `slice` to nothing return `[]`.
5. **A builder is owned.** A builder is a plain array one loop writes with `push` and then hands
   over, once, as a plain list, after which it is never written: `core/List`'s core-private
   `Builder` (below) and the destination of Â§8's tail calls modulo cons. It is used **linearly** â
   every `add` returns the builder, and that result is the only thing the loop uses next â so no
   code other than its loop can see it before the hand-over, and neither Â§9 item 1's dead-binding
   rule nor its single-use inlining can drop or reorder a write. A resumption of a suspended fiber
   is one-shot (`transparent-effects-proposal.md` Â§16.1), which is what makes a builder captured by
   a continuation sound; a multi-shot continuation would have to copy it.
6. **Elements are references.** No operation copies, wraps or rebuilds an element: what comes out
   is `===` what went in (research 38 Â§7's *element identity*).

What these invariants do not permit is the rest of what an array can do in place. In particular a
`set` or `push` whose input is provably unique is still a copy or a new header here; static
in-place writes (research 42's R0) are a later optimisation that would relax invariant 1 only under
a proof, and nothing in this contract depends on them.

#### What a reader of a list may rely on: the protocol

*Superseded 2026-10-15 by *The representation: a plain array* (above), once S7 lands; kept as the record.*

Code that reads a list without being `core/List.js` â a sibling, a platform runtime, the markup
runtime, the derived-comparison engine, `Debug` â may rely on exactly three things, and on no field
name of a view or a trie:

1. **`xs.length`** is the number of elements, in every form.
2. **`Array.isArray(xs)`** is true exactly for the plain form, whose elements are `xs[0 â¦ length â 1]`.
3. Otherwise **`xs.$plain()`** returns a plain array of the elements, which the caller must not
   write. For a trie it is computed once and cached (invariant 1), so a second call on the same
   header is O(1).

The idiom is one line, and every first-party file that reads a list uses it:

```js
const a = Array.isArray(xs) ? xs : xs.$plain();
```

**A value is a list exactly when `Array.isArray(v) || typeof v.$plain === "function"`.** No other
beni value is a JavaScript array (a tuple is `{a, b, â¦}`, Â§4), and no record can have a field called
`$plain` (a field name is a lower-case identifier), which is how `Debug.toString` tells a list from
anything else.

`$plain` is a **field** holding one shared function expression â `$plain: TriePlain` in the header
literal, reading `this` â and not a prototype method. `Minify` declines a file that mentions `class`
or holds a top-level expression statement such as `T.prototype.m = â¦` (Â§9, *Hand-written JavaScript
under `--release`*), and no file in `core/` may be declined. Property names are never renamed by
Â§9's passes (a key before `:` and a property after `.` are not bindings), so `length`, `$plain` and
`push` survive every build.

What a sibling may **return** as a list is [`boundary.md`](boundary.md) Â§4's: a fresh plain array
that nothing else holds and that it never touches again, or a list it was given.

*Amended 2026-10-01 (E1tp):* **the protocol is unchanged, still three points.** A trie header
carries `length` as a data field â as this contract always said; research 46's E1t prototype called
it `n`, which is why Â§11.2 of that report mentions the change â so `length` and the empty test read
one field on every form. The head, its reversal, the radix offset and the shared tree object are
private to `core/List.js`: no reader sees `off` or `hc`, because `$plain()` returns the elements from
index 0 in order â the head reversed, then the leaves from radix `off`, then the tail cut to this
version's count â and caches the array as E1t's did. Neither claim is a reader's business: only
`core/List.js` writes a head or a tail.

|---|---|---|---|

#### Identity: what an operation returns unchanged

*Amended 2026-10-15 (*The representation: a plain array*, above):* the trie-header bullets below
are withdrawn with the trie. On an in-place platform, a writer that writes returns its input array
itself, edited. The rest stands.

`language.md` Â§11.12 promises that a value a program does not rebuild keeps its identity, and the
markup runtime skips work on `===` (Â§15.5, Â§15.8). For lists that promise is these guarantees, which
research 38 Â§7 measured for the ports this runtime is built from, and which `core/List` documents as
guarantees on each function:

- **The input itself**, not an equal copy, from: `set`, `update` and `swap` out of range or writing
  the identical value (`===`, not `==`) and `swap xs i i`; `insertAt` and `removeAt` out of range;
  `slice` and `take` covering the whole list, `drop xs 0` and `view xs 0`; `xs ++ []` and
  `[] ++ ys`; `filter` keeping every element; `map` and `indexedMap` when every result is `===` its
  element (one comparison per element â the result built is dropped); `reverse`, `sort`, `sortBy`
  and `sortWith` of fewer than two elements; `pop []`; `concat` and `concatMap` when exactly one
  list is non-empty (that list). The last replaces the cons list's sharing of a tail, which an
  array cannot do: `append` no longer shares its second list, and `concat` no longer shares its
  last non-empty list unless it is the only one.

  *Amended 2026-10-13 (the owner's decision, `language.md` Â§6.8, *What an operation returns
  unchanged*): the functions that build no longer return their input.* `slice` and `take` covering
  the whole list, `xs ++ []` and `[] ++ ys` (`append`, both spellings), `filter` keeping every
  element, `map` and `indexedMap` when every result is `===` its element, `reverse`, `sort`,
  `sortBy` and `sortWith` of fewer than two elements, and `concat` and `concatMap` when exactly one
  list is non-empty **return a fresh list**, each at the cost its row states; `append` with an empty
  side is a plain copy of the other, O(its length), and never converts a plain list to a trie.
  `map` and `indexedMap` lose their per-element comparison and the core-private `identical` and
  `kept` that carried it (`ownership-checker.md` Â§27). The rest of the first bullet stands: the
  writers out of range or writing the identical value, `swap xs i i`, `pop []`, and `drop xs 0` and
  `view xs 0`, which return their input as a writer and a view do. The reason is the ownership

  compare elements).
- **Element identity** always (invariant 6).
- **A view is the same list as another view of the same backing array at the same offset.** Two
  matches of `x :: rest` against one list bind two view objects, and `===` tells them apart where
  the cons list's `rest` was one cell. The markup runtime therefore compares with `same(a, b)` â

- *Added 2026-10-01 (E1tp):* **a prepend that re-conses a view gives back the wider list.**
  `cons(x, t)` where `t` is a view of `b` at `o` and `b[o â 1] === x` is the view of `b` at

*Amended 2026-10-15 (*The representation: a plain array*, above):* on an in-place platform, a

| beni | JavaScript |
|---|---|

No list carries a `$` tag, so no list test is a tag test and nothing in Â§4's constructor rows or

#### `--release`, the hoisted file and the read/write split

*Superseded 2026-10-15 by *The representation: a plain array* (above), once S7 lands; kept as the record.*

- **The list primitives are `pure` `foreign`s** (`boundary.md` Â§4's rung), so Â§9 item 1 treats a
  call of one as it treats any pure call: an unused `view` or `unsafeGet` binding is dropped in
  `--release` (the development build does not bind an unread tail in the first place, Â§7). The
  builder's `add` is declared `pure` too, which is sound only because of invariant 5's linearity;
  `List.beni` is the one place that may call it, and every call's result is the builder its loop
  passes on. A `$root.push(â¦)` statement that Â§8 writes is a method call on a local and is never
  dropped.
- **`core/List.js` is hoistable** into Â§9's one file: no `class`, no top-level expression statement,
  every top-level initialiser inert (literals, arrows, function expressions, objects and arrays of
  them), each export `export const f = (â¦) =>` with its parameter list written out (`boundary.md`
  Â§4 check 4). `Minify`'s unit test that no file of `core/` is declined covers it.
- **Readers never name write code** (research 40 Â§5 and Â§8's rules). A trie is born only in a writer
  (`set`, `push`, `pop`, `swap`; `update` is `set`), so the trie's write half â path copies, the
  build from a plain array, the tail claim, leaf push and pop â is mentioned by writers alone, and a
  program that imports no writer ships none of it (research 40 measured 452 bytes brotli for a
  read-only program's adaptive sibling against 901 for one that writes). Whether the trie's **read**
  half (the descent `unsafeGet` needs and the flatten `$plain` runs) can go too, through the header's
  own field, is measured in `plans/list-arrays.md`'s last slice; research 40 Â§5 rule 2 found a hot
  read through an indirection 15â18 % slower, so it is not assumed.
  *Amended 2026-10-01 (E1tp):* **`cons` and `append` are writers now**: a prepend onto 32 elements
  or more is where a trie is born, so the conversion, the head claim, the head-to-leaf placement and
  the root's left growth are mentioned by `cons`, and every program that writes `[ x, ...xs ]` as
  an expression ships the trie's write half, where under E1t only `set`, `push`, `pop` and `swap`
  pulled it in. `view`'s trie branch â the header arithmetic and the reversed copy of a leaf's rest
  into a head â is read-side code and is small. The slice that measures the read/write split
  (`plans/list-arrays.md`'s last) measures a program that only prepends as its own case.
  *Amended 2026-10-11:* **`cons` is a reader again** â with no head claim, no left growth and no
  conversion it only reads (a re-cons test, `$plain()`) â so a program that prepends and never
  pushes, sets or appends ships none of the trie's write half. `append` stays a writer.
- **Research 40 Â§8's other rules** apply to the file as written: one walk written once, parameters
  named by role, capitalised top-level names and lower-case locals, every speed-motivated line
  commented with its reason.

#### What is not done

*Superseded 2026-10-15 by *The representation: a plain array* (above), once S7 lands; kept as the record.*

- **No front buffer** (research 38 Â§17.2's E2): prepending is O(n), and no measured array-first
  program prepends. *Withdrawn 2026-10-01 by the owner's E1tp amendment:* the claimable head is
  that buffer, because Elm-style programs do prepend (research 46 Â§11). *Restored 2026-10-11 by
  the owner:* there is no front buffer again â prepending is O(n) because the language must not
  reward it, and `prepend_in_loop` names the loops that do it (*The claimable head: E1tp*,
  amended).
- *Added 2026-10-01 (E1tp):* **No prefix levels.** Scala 2.13's `Vector` keeps `prefix1 â¦
  prefixN-1` arrays and running counts per level, one class per depth and a comparison against the
  counts on every read (research 46 Â§11.1). E1tp keeps one head buffer and moves the radix offset
  instead, so a full head becomes a whole leaf, indexing needs no counts, and there is one header
  shape.
- *Added 2026-10-01 (E1tp):* **No claim on `append`'s plain half or on `++`.** `++` is
  `Basics.append`, a sibling that cannot reach the trie (above), and a concatenation of two long
  plain lists is a fresh plain array, as under E1t; only `core/List`'s `append` pushes, and only
  when it can do so in amortised O(1) per element.
- **No O(log n) `slice`, `concat` or `insertAt`** (funkia's RRB tree, research 46 Â§9): 2.9Ã the
  bytes and 1.2â2.5Ã slower reads everywhere.
- **No conversion functions in beni.** There is no JavaScript-array type in the language to convert
  to; a list crosses the boundary through a sibling or a port, under the protocol.
- **No static in-place writes** (research 42's R0), above.

### A record literal's keys move; its initialisers do not

The sorted key order above is a **representation** decision and `language.md` Â§6's *Evaluation
order* is a **semantic** one, and where they meet the semantics wins: `{ zed = p, alpha = q }`
emits `{alpha: â¦, zed: â¦}` and runs `p` before `q`. So the emitter sorts a permutation of the
fields, lowers the initialisers in the order they are **written**, and binds one to a `const $t$<n>`
before the object literal whenever leaving it in place would move its evaluation. The first backend sorted the
fields and then lowered each one, which ran them in key order; the fixtures are
`run/EvalOrderRecordFields.beni` and `emit/RecordFieldOrder.js`.

**A temporary is bought only where one is needed**, because an unnecessary one is bytes in every
record literal in the program. Two things can move an evaluation, and an **atom** â a literal, a
name, or the `$t$<n>` a `case` has already assigned â is moved by neither, since re-reading one
repeats no work and shows nothing:

| The literal | What is pinned |
|---|---|
| already in key order, no initialiser hoisting statements | nothing: the initialisers stay inside the object literal, byte for byte as before |
| the sort moves the fields, and **at most one** initialiser is not an atom | nothing: one evaluation cannot be reordered against values that are only read |
| the sort moves the fields, and two or more initialisers are not atoms | every non-atom, to a `const` in written order; the object reads the names |
| some initialiser lowers to **statements** (a `case`, an `?`) | every non-atom written before the last such initialiser â its statements run before the object literal is built, so what is written in front of it has to have run already |

The rule is deliberately conservative: it pins by the *shape* of the lowered value and never asks
whether a particular expression could be observed. The same rule holds wherever an emitted order
can differ from a written one, which is why Â§7's tree rebuilds occurrences rather than re-evaluating
subjects, and why record **update** needed nothing: a spread moves no initialiser.

### `?` is a test and a `return`, and the statements around it

`language.md` Â§6.6's `e?` yields the payload of an `Ok`/`Just` and returns the `Err`/`Nothing` from
the enclosing function. It is three pieces of JavaScript, and no `case`:

```js
const $t$1 = String$toInt(text);            // the subject, evaluated exactly once
if ($t$1.$ === "Nothing") return $t$1;      // the failure test, and the early return
â¦$t$1.aâ¦                                    // the value of the expression
```

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| the subject | evaluated **once** (`language.md` Â§6) and bound to a `$t$<n>`, because the test and the payload both read it. A subject that is already an atom â a name, a literal â is read twice instead and nothing is bound |
| the test | `<subject>.$ === "<failure tag>"` for Â§4's padded representation, `<subject> === "<failure tag>"` for a bare tag. The failing constructor is `Nothing` for the `Maybe` shape and `Err` for the `Result` one, and its representation is looked up like any other constructor's, from the declaring module's interface |
| **which shape** | the CHECKER's, carried in the dispatch table (`checker.md` Â§6.5, `static-dispatch-spike.md` Â§7.1). The emitter sees no types (Â§3) and a `?` carries no pattern, so this is the one thing about it the backend cannot work out; a `?` with no row is `internal` and stops the build |
| the failure | **the subject itself, returned unchanged.** Nothing is rebuilt and nothing new is named |
| the value | the payload slot, which is slot 0 â `a` â for `Just` and for `Ok` alike |

**Returning the subject is sound because neither failure carries the type that changed.** `?` takes
a `Result e a` inside a function answering `Result e b`: an `Err` holds an `e` and never an `a`, so
the object that came in is already the object that goes out, and re-wrapping it would allocate a
second one with the same two fields. `Maybe a` to `Maybe b` is the same argument with an empty
hand: Â§4's padding makes `Nothing` a `{$:"Nothing",a:null}` whatever `a` was. This is also what
keeps Â§9 honest â the failure path names no declaration, imports nothing and adds no edge, so a
`?` cannot keep anything alive.

**The `return` is the enclosing function's, wherever the statement lands.** `language.md` Â§6.6 says
a `?` returns from the nearest enclosing *definition with parameters* and makes a lambda in between
`question_in_lambda`, so there is no case where the beni answer and the JavaScript answer could
differ: a `let` definition with parameters is its own emitted `function` (Â§8's cases table), a
parameterless `let` binding is a `const` in the enclosing one, and a lambda cannot be reached. A
`return` inside Â§7's labelled block or `switch` leaves the function and not the block â that is
what distinguishes it from a leaf's `break $c$<d>`, which is how a leaf delivers the `case`'s own
value â and inside Â§8's `while (true)` it leaves the loop with the function.

**Everything written before a `?` must have run before it.** The early `return` is a statement, so
it runs where the statements go, ahead of the expression it was written inside; an expression
written to its left that is still sitting in that expression would run *after* it, or â if the `?`
fails â not at all. This is the record literal's rule above, generalised: **a run of
sub-expressions in written order pins to a `const` every non-atomic value written before the last
one that hoists statements.** It applies to every position that holds more than one written
expression â a call's arguments *together with its callee*, a method call's receiver and
arguments, a constructor's arguments, a list, a tuple, an interpolation's segments, a record
literal's initialisers, a record update's base and fields â and it is the same machinery, so a
`case` in the same position was fixed by the same change. Short-circuit `&&`/`||` need nothing
extra: correction 3 above already gives the right operand its own branch, and statements hoisted
there run only when it does.

Two consequences worth stating, because they are what the emitted shape looks like:

- **In a `case` (Â§7)**, a `?` in a branch body hoists into *that branch* and nowhere else, so the
  other branch does not run its test; a `?` in the scrutinee hoists before the tree, once. A leaf
  that hoists statements is why the conditional-expression shape is chosen only after the bodies
  are lowered: `a ? b : c` cannot hold a `return`, and the tree falls back to the statement form.
- **In a looping function (Â§8)**, a `?` in a **tail-call argument** is not in tail position â the
  operand of a `?` never is â so it is evaluated with the other arguments, before any parameter is
  rebound, and its failure returns out of the loop rather than continuing it.

### Emitted JavaScript nests only as deep as the source

*Added 2026-09-25.* Every JavaScript engine parses â and V8 and JavaScriptCore
compile â a nested expression or block by recursion, and gives up with `RangeError` or
`InternalError` past a depth that depends on the construct and the engine. Before this section a
program the compiler accepted could lower to a module no engine would load: a list literal was one
object per element each inside the last, `a + b + â¦` one `Basics$add` call per term, `++` and `::`
the same, and `&&` printed as `a && (b && â¦)`. `build` exited 0 and the module threw while it was
being parsed â from about 1 550 levels in Node, 1 290 in Chrome, 860 in the SpiderMonkey shell. The
parser's own budget (`language.md` Â§10, 4 096 charges a declaration) sits above every one of those
numbers, and does not charge a list's elements at all.

The rule is two halves. **A form the source writes FLAT is emitted flat, however long it is**: its
nesting in JavaScript may not grow with its length. **Nesting the source writes itself is carried
into JavaScript up to a budget the engines can load, and refused by name past it** â which, since
everything flat is flat, is only ever functions and `case`s nested inside one another scores deep.

**What the engines load, measured.** Each figure is the deepest (or widest) the engine loads and
runs, found by a binary search to 1 % over generated modules: `import()` of a `blob:` URL in the
three browsers (headless, Linux x86-64), a `data:` URL in Node, `new Function` in the two shells,
2026-09-25. `â¥` is the top of the search. The browser figures are what a page gets; the shells are
the engines alone, and the SpiderMonkey shell runs on a smaller stack than Firefox does.

| Construct, one level | Chrome 153 | Firefox 144 | WebKit (WPE, Safari 605.1.15) | Node 24.19 | SpiderMonkey 140 shell | Bun 1.3.13 (JSC) |

| `x && (x && â¦)` | 1 006 | 1 437 | 3 323 | 1 510 | 897 | 3 121 |
| alternate `c ? 0 : c ? 0 : â¦` | â¥ 300 000 | 4 147 | 6 563 | â¥ 300 000 | 2 151 | 6 710 |
| consequent `c ? (c ? â¦ : 0) : 0` | 1 281 | 4 147 | 6 563 | 1 876 | 2 151 | 6 710 |
| `if (c) { return 0; } else { â¦ }` | 644 | 1 931 | 3 964 | 1 519 | 759 | 2 297 |
| `if (c) { â¦ } else if (c) â¦` | 1 290 | â¥ 300 000 | 35 750 | 3 891 | â¥ 300 000 | 32 234 |
| `switch (k) { case 0: { â¦ } }` | 595 | 726 | 3 707 | 1 024 | 358 | 1 913 |
| `{ â¦ }` | 1 308 | 3 525 | 7 626 | 2 480 | 1 235 | 3 488 |
| `{ let a = 1; â¦ }` | 1 290 | **251** | 7 626 | 2 499 | **251** | â |

| flat `x && x && â¦`, terms | â¥ 300 000 | â¥ 300 000 | 53 620 | â¥ 300 000 | â¥ 300 000 | 53 620 |
| flat `x + x + â¦`, terms | â¥ 300 000 | â¥ 300 000 | 40 144 | â¥ 300 000 | â¥ 300 000 | 29 304 |

Three things in that table decide the design. **There are two limits, not one.** Every engine runs
out of stack, at a depth that depends on the construct; SpiderMonkey also refuses a 252nd nested
scope â braces that declare something, or a function â with "function nested too deeply", in the
shell and in Firefox alike, **whatever stack is left**. In a module a function with a declaring body
reaches it at 171. **The scarcest browser is not one browser**: Chrome for calls, `if` blocks and
`switch`, Firefox for objects, arrows and scopes. **A flat chain is not free in JavaScriptCore**,
which nests `a && b && c` where V8 builds one n-ary node and SpiderMonkey loops; it still loads
53 620 terms. Mobile builds of these engines were not measured, and their stacks may be smaller â
the margins below are the answer to that, not a measurement of it.

**The unit and the budgets** (`JsIr.nesting`, `JsIr.Builder.measure`). A path from a declaration
down to a leaf costs the sum of what each construct on it costs; the unit is a quarter of a nested
call, so that the scarcest browser's call depth, Chrome's 1 290, is 5 160 units, and every weight is
5 160 over the scarcest browser-or-Node depth of its construct, rounded up:

| Weight | Units | Scarcest depth |
|---|---|---|
| call â callee and each argument | 4 | Chrome, 1 290 |
| object literal â each property's value | 5 | Firefox, 1 263 |
| array literal | 4 | â |
| member, index, unary, template hole | 2 | not measured; never deeper than the source |
| binary operand; a left operand only when it is not the same-precedence chain | 6 | Chrome, 1 006 with parentheses |
| left operand of a same-precedence chain, printed without parentheses | 0 | V8 and SpiderMonkey: none |
| conditional test and consequent | 5 | Chrome, 1 281 |
| conditional alternate | 2 | Firefox, 4 147 |
| function body (`=>`, `function`) | 7 | Firefox, 497 as `(() => â¦)()`, with the call's 4 |
| `if` and its braces | 9 | Chrome, 644 |
| `{ â¦ }` | 4 | Chrome, 1 290 |
| `switch`, before its case's braces | 5 | Chrome, 595 with the braces |
| `while (true) { â¦ }` | 9 | as `if` |
| any other statement | 1 | â |

Every top-level declaration may cost at most **2 048 units** (`nesting.budget`: 512 nested calls,
two and a half times under the browsers' edge and one and a half under the SpiderMonkey shell's)
and nest at most **128 scopes** (`nesting.scope_budget`: half of SpiderMonkey's 251). A function is
one scope and braces that declare something one more.

**The shapes.** Each long form, and what it is now. Every `run/`, `emit/` and `emit/release/` golden
of the corpus was byte-identical; the emitted JavaScript itself moved in two ways, stdout
identical everywhere. `&&`/`||` of three terms or more prints flat at any length (`_core/Char.mjs`'s
`isHexDigit` and `isAlphaNum`), and a list literal past 32 elements is an array (`run/CharOps`,
`CoreCharRest`, `CoreMaybeResultRest`, `CoreNumericExtremes`, `CoreStringRest`, `Int32Bits` and
`ReleaseEverything`); the goldens hold because they are stdout, or the fixture's own module.

| Form | Was | Is |
|---|---|---|
| list literal, up to 32 elements | nested cells | unchanged |
| list literal, 33 or more (`max_cons_elements`) | one nested object per element | `[e1, e2, â¦].reduceRight(($l, $h) => ({ $: 1, a: $h, b: $l }), { $: 0, a: null, b: null })` |
| `&&` / `\|\|` chain | `a && (b && (c && d))` | `a && b && c && d`, one run |
| `&&` / `\|\|` chain whose operands need statements | `let $t; if (a) { â¦; $t = b && â¦; } else { $t = false; }`, one more `if` inside for each such operand | `let $t = a; if ($t) { â¦b's statements; $t = b; } if ($t) { â¦; $t = c; }` â one flat `if` per such operand (`if (!$t)` for `\|\|`), the operands without statements riding in the assignment before them |
| a lambda whose body is 128 units tall (`lambda_spill`) | the closure inline, where it is an argument | the closure bound to `const $t$<n>` where it is made, so the call it is an argument of nests none of it |
| derived `==` over a record or payload | `$m$0(â¦) && $m$1(â¦) && â¦`, one run | the same, in runs of 1 024 terms joined as `â¦ && (â¦) && (â¦)` (`derived_group`), so JavaScriptCore nests at most 1 024 and the number of runs |
| `+ - * / ++ :: \|> <\|`, nested calls, records, tuples, constructors | one call or object per level | the same until the expression is `nesting.spill` tall (256 units, 51 to 64 levels), then that much is bound to `const $t$<n>` in front of it, and the chain goes on from the name |
| `else if` chain in a function's result, 16 `if`s or more (`chain_min`) | one `if`/`else` inside the last | `if (a) { return â¦; }` then the next test, one after another |
| `else if` chain in an expression, 16 `if`s or more | one `let $t$<n>` and `if`/`else` inside the last | one `$c$<d>: { â¦ }` block and one temporary: `if (a) { $t = â¦; break $c$<d>; }`, one after another |
| `if`s each in the `then` branch of the one before, 16 or more, either position | the same, nested the other way | the same, flat, each test negated so that the short `else` is inside and the chain follows: `if (x.$ !== "Just") { return 0; }` |
| evidence for a type nested *n* deep | one closure per level, `(x, y) => List$eq((x, y) => â¦, x, y)` | a closure 20 levels deep (`evidence_spill`) is bound to a `const` ahead of the call |
| string interpolation, record literal, `case` of literals | flat already | unchanged |

*Amended 2026-10-01:* the two list-literal rows go with the cons cell (*Lists are arrays*, above).
An array literal nests at no length, so every list literal is the "flat already" row, and
`max_cons_elements`, the `reduceRight` step and `run/NestingFlatList`'s claim about cell shapes are
withdrawn when `plans/list-arrays.md`'s second slice lands; the fixture keeps its output.

**Why none of this moves an evaluation** (`language.md` Â§6 is normative). A spilled `const` goes
where a `case` or a `?` in the same position would put its statements â `Lower.expr`'s `out`, the
statement list in front of the expression â so it runs exactly where the value would have been
evaluated, and every caller that holds a run of written-order values already pins the ones written
before a hoist (`orderedExprs`, *`?` is a test and a `return`* above). A branch of a short circuit or
of a `case` has an `out` of its own, so a spill never runs anything the source would not have. A
flat list's elements are an array literal's, evaluated left to right as the nested cells' were, and
its cells are the same `{$, a, b}` in the same key order, so they share the cons cell's hidden class
(Â§9.4). `&&` and `||` are associative in value and in evaluation â the first falsy (truthy) operand
decides and nothing after it runs â so `a && (b && c)` and `a && b && c` are one program; an operand
that needs statements runs them only inside `if ($t)`, which holds exactly when every operand before
it said so, so nothing runs that the nested form would not have run. A flat `else if` chain works
because every arm leaves â a `return` in tail position, a `break` out of the chain's block in an
expression â so what followed the `else` inside it may follow the `if` instead. An evidence closure
is hoisted only when it is an arrow: making a closure runs nothing, where the evidence applied to a
constant (A.85) is a call and stays where it is. For the same reason a hoist that is nothing but
`const`s of closures â evidence, or a lambda bound where it is made â pins nothing written before it
(`onlyClosures`): the values in front stay inline and still run first. `run/NestingFlatList.beni`, `NestingChains.beni`,
`NestingElseIf.beni`, `NestingEvidence.beni` and `NestingLogicalStatements.beni` log every operand,
and `ViewMap20x30`, `ViewMap40x12` and `ViewMapEvery3` are TEA-style `view`s with a `List.map` lambda
at every level or every third; each was confirmed against its
oracle twin, the same program built by the compiler before this section. `emit/NestingShapes.beni` holds the shapes.

**How the lowering knows.** Cheaply, where it decides, and exactly where it refuses:

- `Lower.expr` keeps a running maximum, `expr_height`, of the expressions lowered inside the one it
  is lowering, and adds the instruction's own weight: one addition per expression, no walk. A
  `let`'s bindings are statements and do not count toward it, and a value that came back an atom
  counts nothing. A lambda's body DOES count: it nests inside whatever the lambda is an argument of
  (a review found a `view` of twenty `List.map`s refused), and once it is
  `lambda_spill` tall the closure is bound where it is made. Evidence keeps its own count, in
  closures.
- A chain is counted by following, from each `case`, the last branch whose body is another `case`
  under any `let`s (`leafCaseDepth`), up to `chain_min`. Of the two branches of each test, the one
  with more nodes follows the `if`.
- `refuseTooDeep` measures each top-level declaration's statements exactly, by one walk over an
  explicit stack (`JsIr.Builder.measure`), and only when the declaration built at least
  `nesting.could_exceed` nodes â 128, fewer than which no statement can be over either budget.

**What is refused, and why a refusal is right there.** A declaration over either budget is
`nesting_too_deep` (`language.md` Â§10), naming the declaration, both measures and both limits, and
nothing is written. After everything above, only nesting the program writes itself can get there:
120 functions each applied inside the last, a TEA `view` with a `List.map` lambda at every level 65
to 69 levels deep (at 30 and at 12 children a level), or about 150 `case`s or `if`s each inside an
ARGUMENT of a call inside the one before â `f (if b then f (if b then â¦ else 0) else 0)` â where no
branch is left for the next test to follow. Every lambda costs a scope, and one bound where it is
made makes its enclosing body declare something, a second; 128 scopes is what bounds these. CLAUDE.md rule 7 allows a refusal only where the guarantee at stake â no
runtime exception â has no correct emission to keep it, and for these there is none short of a
different compiler: a function scope is how JavaScript closes over its variables, and taking one
out means closure conversion, every captured variable moved into an environment object; a `case`
inside an argument has to be finished before the call it is an argument of, and taking its blocks
out means turning expressions into a jump-threaded statement machine. Either reshapes every
program's output to rescue source nobody writes, and the parser already refuses nesting past 4 096
on the same principle. The budgets sit two and a half times under the scarcest browser, so the
refusal comes well before any engine's edge and not at it. What must never happen, and does not,
is a flat form refused. `abuse_test.zig` holds the edge: 119 nested functions run, 120 are refused.

**The wide form, measured in browsers** (`static-dispatch-spike.md` Â§9.2, A.87). A function of *n*
parameters called with *n* arguments loads and runs up to 59 610 in Chrome and Node, 65 078 in
Firefox and the SpiderMonkey shell, and past 70 000 in WebKit and Bun. `Convention.max_positional_evidence`
stays at 4 096, fourteen times under the scarcest for ONE call. Under recursion the frames add up
(Node, default stack, a self-recursive arrow with *n* extra parameters): 16
extra parameters recurse 2 928 deep, 256 recurse 237, 1 024 recurse 59 and 4 096 only 13. So a
recursive nominal type whose payload has exactly 4 096 fields â the positional form â overflows
`==` about 13 levels down, where 4 097 fields â the array form â does not. No program the corpus
knows is near it; the caveat is recorded in `static-dispatch-spike.md` Â§9.2 and A.87. *Since 2026-09-27
neither overflows at any depth (*Derived comparisons do not grow the native stack*, below).*

**Cost.** Emit, ReleaseFast `zig build bench -- --generate=100000`, medians of seven interleaved
runs, four sets: +1.9 %, +0.4 %, and after the review's fixes 52.64 against 51.77 (+1.7 %) and 52.70
against 52.84 (â0.3 %); the review measured +2.9 %. It is noise-bound around +1 %, inside the Â±3 %.
The bench program's JavaScript is 4 bytes shorter. Output size (`bench/size.mjs`): `bench/corpus` 128 437 â 128 431 bytes raw, 22 478 â 22 483
brotli, release 15 651 â 15 643 brotli; the `emit/` corpus unchanged; across `run/`, a program with a
long list literal is 500â900 bytes smaller raw and within Â±12 bytes brotli, since nested cells
compress very well.

**Known gaps.** A `case` of more than 65 046 literal branches was one `switch` SpiderMonkey refuses;
*closed 2026-09-27:* a fan of more than 16 384 labels is consecutive `switch`es
(Â§7, *The emitted shape*). Mobile engines are unmeasured. A lambda applied on the spot, `(Î»x -> â¦) a`, costs a
function scope where a `let` would cost none; lowering it as the `let` it means would lift the
120-function edge. Evidence nested inside a deep expression is counted by the
exact measure and not by the cheap one, so it can be refused where binding more of it would have
loaded.

**Schema declarations** additionally produce an inspectable description and
ordinary specialised top-level parse/print functions, with both success and

Â§5 owns the context contract shared with the library interpreter. This is a
specified fork, not implemented code or an effects-runtime decision.
*(Amended 2026-10-02: built â `schema.md` Â§6, *The specialised path, as specified for S4*, and Â§16,
*As built â S4*: `src/js/SchemaLower.zig` writes it, and Â§9's walk has a schema member node.)*
